Let V be a symplectic vector space, and let Omega denote its symplectic form. A fundamental question arises: can non-trivial alterations of zero make the product of two symplectic forms, V x W with form Omega x Pi, into a new form that preserves the symplectic structure? The answer provided in this study is affirmative under certain conditions. Specifically, if V and W have sufficiently high dimensions (at least 10 dimensions), there exist alterations I and J such that the altered spaces V^I and W^J, when combined, can be equipped with a new symplectic form that maintains the original relationship. The proof of this assertion relies heavily on techniques from h-principle theory, particularly the h-principle for the corank one Legendrian contact homogenization.

The entity suggestion task involves utilizing text from a knowledge base to propose corresponding entities within text documents. To effectively accomplish this task, it is crucial to leverage the hierarchical and layered structure of Wikipedia, which organizes pages into a multi-layered graph representation. In this study, we present a novel approach to entity suggestion by employing a Wikipedia-based layered graph embedding method. Our method involves training a k-hop sampling classifier to capture the hierarchical structure of Wikipedia pages and then utilizing this classifier to train a suggestion model. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in improving entity suggestion performance.

The concept of ideal incompatible kidney transplants has been proposed to address the issue of crossmatch incompatibility, a significant barrier to finding suitable donors for patients on the waiting list. A nationwide survey was conducted to gauge the level of support for this groundbreaking idea among nephrologists, transplant surgeons, and primary care physicians in Italy. Participants were presented with a hypothetical scenario involving a patient awaiting a kidney transplant and asked to rate their willingness to accept an incompatible kidney from a donor who had not been previously matched with the recipient. The results indicated that 60% of physicians would consider accepting an incompatible kidney transplant, with 20% expressing strong support. Notably, there were no significant differences in responses based on the level of training or specialty of the physicians surveyed. The findings suggest that a substantial proportion of physicians are open to the idea of ideal incompatible kidney transplants, highlighting the potential for expanding the kidney transplant waiting list and reducing the number of deceased donor transplants.

This paper provides an overview of the implicit kernel approach, a method for
reproducing complex functions without explicit formula derivation. It outlines
theoretical underpinnings, applications in computing special functions and solving
differential equations, as well as alternative techniques within this framework.

This paper challenges the common perception that modern word representations have a deep understanding of the semantic characteristics of financial documents. To investigate this issue, we focus on the Loughran-McDonald taxonomy of positive and negative emotions and examine the quality of word representations in capturing this quality. Initially, we explore whether our basic word representations can accurately predict whether an emotion is positive or negative. Subsequently, we employ a neural network to classify words based on their emotional content. Our findings indicate that while certain high-frequency words with clear positive or negative sentiments are easily classified, the majority of words are difficult to classify with significant accuracy. Furthermore, we find that using contextualized word representations yields only marginal improvements over non-contextualized ones.

To make it easier for readers to grasp the main contribution of having multiple antennas and using multiple carriers, this work presents an alternative method of achieving extra benefit in integrated data and power transfer through a single channel, using a single antenna. The proposed method involves employing a unique type of waveform that spans a wide bandwidth, which can be realized via a single antenna. By applying a unified analytical framework to both this proposed waveform and OFDM, we can compare the performance of different transmission systems. The results of this comparison show that, under certain conditions, a system using multiple transmitters and carriers can achieve the same integrated data and power transfer as either a single transmitter with a wide bandwidth system or a system using multiple transmitters and carriers with orthogonal frequency division multiplexing.

This research presents a novel numerical method for solving complex Stefan problems that involve multiple interfaces and material components with varying physical properties. The method utilizes the level-set technique to track interface dynamics and the embedded boundary technique to model the domain geometry and material properties. By integrating these approaches, the method effectively handles problems with large deformations, interface merging and splitting, and irregular geometries. The embedded boundary technique employs a finite element formulation that accurately captures the behavior of the interface and the surrounding fluid. The method's efficiency is enhanced through the use of adaptive mesh refinement techniques and parallel computing. Numerical simulations demonstrate the method's accuracy and reliability in solving a range of solidification-melt problems, including dendritic growth, droplet freezing, and flow-induced phase changes.

One word phrases in the English language are known as one-word sentences.  This study focuses on a particular category of one-word sentences that contain an ancient linguistic structure called the reflexive or reciprocal pronoun.  These pronouns, which are usually dependent on other words, are being interpreted through the lens of quantum natural language, a theoretical framework that applies the principles of quantum mechanics to the study of language.  By examining the quantum states of languages, researchers have discovered that these pronouns can create distinct, isolated quantum states that are separate from the classical interpretation of language.  This finding suggests that the traditional understanding of language may be too limited to fully capture the complexity of human communication.

In games where players make decisions based on uncertain beliefs about each other's actions, rational choices can lead to the establishment of equilibria. However, there is no known method to guarantee reaching such a point in games with more than two players. We investigate methods to achieve rationalizable epsilon Nash equilibria in such scenarios. A simple approach we examine is providing players with the ability to suggest strategies and being selected to execute them, but we show this is insufficient. Another approach we explore is a competition where players are rewarded for predicting the actions of others, but we demonstrate this also fails. A solution we propose is a competition where players suggest strategies and being selected to execute them, but we show this method can achieve the desired outcome. We also discuss the practical implications of this approach and its efficiency.

The concept of preventive restructuring has been legally recognized in numerous jurisdictions, including the United States through the Chapter 11 of the bankruptcy code, and in the European Union through the European Preventive Restructuring Directive. This legal framework enables financially distressed companies to reorganize their operations without the need for liquidation. The primary objective of this study is to examine the impact of preventive restructuring on the spread of epidemics within modern organizations. A mathematical model has been developed to analyze the transmission dynamics of infectious diseases in organizations subject to preventive restructuring, and it has been demonstrated that this legal framework can significantly reduce the spread of epidemics. Furthermore, optimal control strategies have been established to minimize the number of infected individuals within organizations.

This research focuses on the geometric properties of a specific type of manifold, the nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold, and examines how Cotton vectors and solitons interact within the context of these manifolds. More specifically, we investigate the conditions under which a pair of linearly independent vector fields can form a Cotton soliton on a nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold, and it is proven that such a condition cannot be satisfied.

This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the framework used in fitting parton distribution functions (PDFs) to experimental data. It delves into the statistical methods employed in fitting, including the discussion of key parameters such as $\chi^2$, covariance matrices, and data weighting. Various approaches to determining PDF uncertainties are examined, covering both linear and non-linear methods, as well as the impact of theoretical systematics. To facilitate future research, a set of recommendations for the PDF fitting community is proposed.

Reinforcement learning techniques, particularly those involving deep neural networks, have been successfully applied to complex decision-making tasks. However, the high level of data demand associated with these techniques poses a significant challenge. One strategy to mitigate this challenge is incorporating an experience replay mechanism, which enables the utilization of previously collected data alongside new observations. Despite its effectiveness, the traditional experience replay approach treats all past data equally, disregarding its potential value in enhancing policy performance. This study proposes an innovative approach, Variance Decrease based Experience Replay (VDER), which selectively leverages high-variance historical observations to accelerate policy performance gains. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the superiority of VDER over conventional methods, yielding significant improvements in both efficiency and outcome.

We present PyCommute, a Python library that accelerates symbolic computations
of sparse, Hermitian matrices through the use of commuting operator expressions.
PyCommute builds upon libcommute, a C++ framework that represents operators as
polynomial expressions, and provides an efficient and user-friendly interface for
scientific computing. We demonstrate the power of libcommute and PyCommute by
applying them to solve the XXZ spin chain's eigenvalue problem, precisely
determining over 100,000 three-body energy levels of the model.

Our research reveals that conventional band theory fails to accurately describe the electronic configuration of (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ superconductor. By employing resonant x-ray diffraction, we discovered that the conventional band theory's prediction of the electronic configuration is incorrect. Instead, we found that the actual spin-orbit coupled bands are shifted to lower energies, resulting in unoccupied states in the superconducting energy gap. Furthermore, we found that these unoccupied states are crucial for the superconducting mechanism, as they allow for the hybridization of hole and electron pockets, which is essential for the formation of the superconducting state.

Two approaches to the supersymmetric partition function have been examined, specifically the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization technique. A connection between these methods has been established, revealing that the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation is equivalent to integrating the superbosonization differential equation. This finding has been verified through explicit calculations of the supermatrices, including Gaussian and chiral ensembles.

The standard model predicts that top quarks produced through a single top quark process will exhibit longitudinal polarization. This characteristic could be utilized to enhance the sensitivity of future high-luminosity large hadron colliders in measuring the Higgs boson's interactions with the electroweak force. However, the potential for other new physics to affect this interaction must be taken into account. The polarization of the top quark produced through a t-channel process is being studied in greater detail, taking into account the full set of final-state particles. The analysis is based on a precise theoretical calculation of the differential cross-section, which is being validated against existing experimental data from the CMS collaboration. The results show that the top quark is significantly polarized, with a degree of polarization of approximately 0.9, which is observable through the decay of the top quark into a W boson and a top quark. The degree of polarization is also influenced by the kinematic properties of the process, with more polarized top quarks being produced at higher transverse momenta. The analysis is being performed using Monte Carlo simulations, which are being validated against existing experimental data from the CMS collaboration. The metallic state of LaNiO3 films on LaAlO3 substrates was found to have a critical thickness around three unit cells, with the exact point being influenced by the presence of oxygen vacancies. To study this effect, researchers created LaNiO3/LaAlO3 superlattices with varying oxygen vacancy levels. They then used beta-detected NMR to examine the spin-lattice relaxation rate of the superlattices, which showed that the metallic phase of the LaNiO3 layers was controlled by the oxygen vacancies in the LaAlO3 barriers.

In our project, MultiTalk aims to create a sophisticated conversational AI that can engage in a wide range of topics through multi-turn dialogues. By incorporating multiple dimensions of complexity, including the number of conversation branches, subjects, and emotional nuances, we are developing a rigorous benchmark for evaluating the intricacy of multi-topic, multi-turn conversations. To facilitate this evaluation, we have developed a unique dataset called MultiTalk, which features human-human conversations with significant multi-branched structures. To overcome the challenges of recreating these complex conversation patterns, we have designed a novel approach called Graph-Driven Dialogue Data Recreational Engine (G3), which allows us to generate high-quality dialogues that closely mirror the complexity of the original human conversations.

This paper examines how large-scale systems behave in an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) assisted multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) setup, considering signal correlation and practical phase-shift limitations. A mathematical model is developed to account for these constraints and a simplified model is proposed for a more manageable analysis. Through this study, the long-term data rate performance of various signal transmission methods is evaluated and theoretical rate limits are derived. Additionally, the impact of certain factors such as covariance structure, phase-shift limitations, and signal-to-noise ratio on data rate behavior is analyzed and illustrated using numerical examples. The results show that a multiple antenna transmission method outperforms a single antenna method in terms of data rate performance.

We present a novel approach to simulate the evolution of particle systems under modified gravity laws by developing a set of equations that can be solved using the fast multipole method. Our method allows for the computation of global system properties at any point in time, and we demonstrate its efficiency by running simulations of particle systems containing up to $10^6$ particles in three-dimensional space. Our algorithm is based on a hierarchical decomposition of the system into smaller sub-regions, and we derive a specific coupling function that allows us to compute the gravitational force between particles in a computationally efficient manner. Our method is applicable to a wide range of gravitational models, and we show its potential by running simulations under different laws of gravitational force. Our results indicate that our method is computationally efficient and can be used to study the evolution of complex systems under altered gravity laws. Our approach is a significant advancement in the field of numerical relativity and gravitational physics, and we look forward to further developments in this area.

Consider now an ensemble of discrete Cauchy-Riemann vector fields, specifically a random "log-gas", with the reciprocal of their pairwise interaction strength denoted by $\beta$. It is proven that as the discretization scale approaches zero, this system converges to a collection of discrete analytic functions, or "log-gas", with the reciprocal interaction parameter $\beta$ set to $4$. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that a specific measure of this discrete log-gas, characterized by its placement in the upper half-plane and avoidance of the x-axis, is intimately tied to the Gaussian free field with an associated $\delta$-source at the origin, with the free field having a weight of one-half. MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source platform that utilizes 'MediaWiki' as its underlying technology. It enables a group of researchers to collaboratively develop and share their work in real-time, incorporating features such as version history, references, and user talk pages. 'WorkingWiki' has been utilized in multiple research projects, including the RCoTeN and CUREN networks, as well as the 'OpenDrift' and 'OpenDRIFT' projects. Its ability to integrate with external services like GitHub and Overleaf makes it a versatile tool for cutting-edge research.

The behavior of turbulent jet fires in windy conditions is analogous to the reaction of a turbulent jet in a straight wind, and understanding this dynamic is crucial for fire safety. To enhance comprehension of how external influences, such as wind, affect fire behavior, researchers are developing methods to manipulate flames in controlled environments. This study employs a linearized approach to model the impact of acoustic waves on turbulent jet fires, using a simplified representation of the combustion process. By applying acoustic waves at the frequency of a flame's natural oscillation, the study demonstrates how the flames can be controlled, resulting in a reduction in their temperature and brightness, and ultimately leading to the development of a method to sustain flames with reduced energy input.

For the stellar oscillations under study, we employ a new, intuitive representation called "geometric modes," which effectively captures the oscillation patterns in a compact form. This approach uses a coordinate system that directly maps onto the physical space of a star, allowing for a clear and straightforward analysis of its vibrational behavior. Through this method, we can easily visualize the complex oscillation patterns and their spatial distribution, as well as their impact on the star's overall structure. This new perspective is particularly useful for understanding the fundamental properties of modes and their role in the broader context of stellar evolution.

A new method for detecting traveling chimera states in neural networks has been developed using a robust metric that identifies distinct dynamical regions in the network. Building upon this approach, a global policy is proposed to classify the chimera state by leveraging the robust metric and a clustering algorithm, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing methods. The effectiveness of this proposal is demonstrated through the identification of moving chimera states in a one-dimensional ring network. The significance of the robust metric in this context is highlighted, showing its crucial role in the successful detection of these states. The supplementary material provides a detailed explanation of the clustering algorithm used in this study.

A theoretical model has been developed to analyze the ultra-high energy photon flux arriving at Earth from all directions without regard to direction, taking into account the influence of the Sun's magnetic field. The model takes into account the anisotropic high energy photon flux that originates from cosmic rays interacting with the Sun, and calculates how these cosmic rays are deflected by the Sun's magnetic field. By applying an isotropization method, the model determines the energy-dependent flux of ultra-high energy photons that reach Earth. Additionally, the energy range where ultra-high energy photons can be detected as an isotropic flux is calculated. The resulting data from the model can be utilized to inform the design of experiments aimed at detecting ultra-high energy photons near Earth.

Nonlocal gravity theories, which offer an alternative to dark energy, can be reformulated into an equivalent model with local gravity and matter. This reformulation results in nonmetric tetrad nonlocal theories, and the nature of the nonmetric tetrads depends on the type of general relativity connection. When the connection is the Levi-Civita connection, the nonmetric tetrads are nonmetric anholonomic local metric fields. Conversely, when the connection is an arbitrary nonmetric connection, the nonmetric tetrads are nonmetric anholonomic constitutive connections. This research reformulates the nonlocal $f(R)$ gravity into an equivalent model with local metric four-dimensional spacetime and a nonmetric tetrad constitutive connection described by a nonlocal $f(\mathcal{R})$ curvature function. It also derives the corresponding field equations and discusses the nonlocal $f(R)$ Starobinsky inflation model.

Conflicting updates pose a significant challenge to the performance of distributed data storage systems. To mitigate this issue, researchers have developed Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs), which guarantee operation independence but require enlarging operations to include information about conflicts, thereby increasing memory usage and slowing down processing. In response to this limitation, we propose an innovative design framework called Eliminate-Win, which enables conflicts to be avoided for specific types of operations through localized processing, effectively removing them from being propagated to other nodes. For remaining conflicts that cannot be avoided, the framework employs existing CRDT techniques to handle them. We demonstrate the framework's efficacy by re-designing fundamental data structures such as counters, sets, and registers, achieving significant improvements in memory usage and processing time, with up to 2x memory reduction and 3x processing time improvement observed in our experiments.

This study examines 18 diverse human traits, ranging from physical appearance to physiological function, by integrating 1000 Genomes Project data with 1000 Genome Project annotations and conducting 1000 Genome Project association studies. We identify 1000 Genomes features that significantly influence association study results, with 18 features among the top 1000 most important. We categorize these features into five groups: gene expression, splicing, chromatin accessibility, methylation, and variant effects. We highlight 1000 Genomes features linked to specific traits, such as increased gene expression in specific tissues correlating with height, and methylation changes in specific tissues correlating with skin pigmentation. We also identify 1000 Genomes features with multiple associated traits, such as chromatin accessibility in liver correlating with both lipid levels and alcohol metabolism. These findings provide valuable insights for future research on the genetic basis of human traits.

This study delves into the complexities of identifying and analyzing rare events in minor systems during experiments at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The challenges posed by high background noise and limited detection capabilities are examined, along with strategies to overcome these obstacles. The paper specifically investigates the production of heavy exotic particles in such rare scenarios, highlighting the significance of this research in the context of searching for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

This paper extends the research of D. S. Diamond and R. Taylor, exploring connections between (compact, geometric) varieties and algebraic structures (semi)simple over number fields. We specifically focus on varieties defined over finite fields, making an initial attempt to establish a link between these two areas. Drawing from recent work by A. Blumberg, B. Antieau, and T. Balmer, we employ the framework of algebraic geometry to investigate the properties of algebraic varieties. Our study reveals a relationship between the periodicity of an algebra's structure and the existence of specific operations within its associated cohomology ring. We then examine the properties of a particular class of algebras, known as tilting algebras, and demonstrate how their structure gives rise to a specific element of specified degree. Our research also establishes a correspondence between these algebras and certain types of superabundant numbers.

This study delves into the effects of molecular vibration on electronic systems, 
seeking to address the limitations of the standard Haberdier-Hamilton Hamiltonian. 
By applying a simple mechanical model to a diatomic molecule, we derived a 
modified spin-vibration-electron interaction that accounts for inertial forces. 
Our results demonstrate that this inertial interaction can be as significant as 
its non-inertial counterpart, in contrast to previous assumptions. Furthermore, 
we derived explicit formulas for the effective exchange and superexchange 
interactions, in contrast to their static counterparts. These results can be 
applied to various molecular systems, in contrast to isolated atoms.

$\tau$-tilting theory was initially introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten, offering a comprehensive framework that effectively maps the characteristics of $\tau$-tilting modules to combinatorial and geometric properties. This framework has been successfully applied to cluster tilting objects in $(q,1)$-Schreier extensions of path algebras, providing a foundation for further exploration. Given the complexity of $\tau$-tilting theory, this introductory paper aims to present the fundamental concepts and key results in an accessible manner, including detailed discussions on combinatorial and geometric aspects, as well as relevant applications. It also presents an overview of recent advancements in the field.

Understanding how natural language conveys meaning is a longstanding challenge in the field. To investigate this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages human-human conversations, which we believe offer a vast and underutilized dataset for studying language comprehension. We introduce a new method to create NLI datasets from conversational data, which we call Conversation-based Natural Language Inference (CNLI). Our approach filters out unreliable NLI judgments by excluding instances where participants disagree on the semantic interpretation of language. We collected two datasets of increasing size, comprising 1,000 and 2,000 conversations, and found that as conversation length increases, the variety of semantic interpretations people make decreases. We found that people's comprehension of language in conversation aligns with that of a control group of individuals who did not engage in conversation, yet our larger model dataset reveals a notable gap in accuracy when compared to human performance on the CNLI tasks. Human-only models achieve an accuracy of 89.1%, whereas baseline neural models reach 75.4% accuracy. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new class of models that simulate the context of conversation, which significantly improves model accuracy to 84.1%.

Autonomous vehicles require the capability to predict dangerous actions from short video clips, specifically during lane-changing maneuvers. Current methods for action recognition from video inputs are computationally expensive and impractical for integration into real-time camera systems used by autonomous cars. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that transfers segmentation masks to pre-recorded footage, reducing the dimensionality of the data and enabling more efficient processing using Motion-Segment Action Prediction (MSAP) networks. Our method achieves high accuracy in recognizing actions, particularly for difficult-to-predict behaviors like pedestrians crossing the road, all while using a single-stream network that can be deployed on a single GPU in a real-time system.

Researchers have recently observed young, rotating brown dwarfs with extremely high spin rates, which may be close to their mass-shedding limits. To better understand the physical properties of rapidly rotating low-mass objects, we developed a computational model that simulates self-gravitating, rotating spheres of fluid in steady-state conditions. This model takes into account the effects of self-gravity, pressure gradients, centrifugal forces, and thermodynamics, and is based on the use of a polytropic equation of state. We performed a detailed analysis of the model's structure, comparing it to non-rotating models and calculating mass-shedding limits for models with indices of 1.0 to 5.0. Our results show that mass-shedding limits are significantly lower for rapidly rotating models, and that mass-shedding limits are not universal, but rather depend on the model's polytropic index. Additionally, we found that mass-shedding limits are significantly lower for models with higher polytropic indices, and that mass-shedding limits are significantly lower for rapidly rotating models than for non-rotating models. Our results have important implications for our understanding of the physical properties of rapidly rotating low-mass objects, and provide a foundation for future research in this area.

High-precision quantum field theory calculations are crucial in interpreting high-energy physics experiments. However, they are limited by our ability to accurately measure experimental data. As next-generation experiments approach, they will produce an abundance of data, necessitating more sophisticated theoretical calculations. This paper presents a new approach to enhance the efficiency of amplitude calculations by directly incorporating experimental factors into a tailored representation of particle data. Building upon previous methods, this approach is demonstrated through a series of complex simulations involving multiple particles and various types of interactions. The results indicate a substantial improvement in computational speed and accuracy when comparing theoretical predictions to observed data.

Observations of Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) and their afterglows across various wavelengths have shown that their light curves evolve over time in distinct patterns. To better understand this, researchers propose that GRBs and their afterglows follow a sequence of development, where low-energy events indicate early-stage bursters, while high-energy events signify later-stage bursters, with intermediate events representing those in between. This hypothesis is supported by analyzing the properties of 41 well-studied GRBs and their afterglows using a K-means clustering algorithm, which revealed that the bursts can be grouped into five categories based on their energy levels and the stage they are in. The analysis also uncovered correlations between GRB properties and their surrounding environments, providing further evidence for the proposed progression of GRB light curves.

Bipartite vertex division involves partitioning a bipartite graph's edges into two disjoint sets, such that one set forms a subset with a bounded size and the other set maintains a bipartite structure. This problem becomes tractable when considering instances where the graph has a bounded complexity relative to a specific parameter. This paper presents a new approach to solving vertex division in bipartite graphs, focusing on tree-decompositions and providing a solution that maintains a specific complexity structure. The proposed approach is then applied to resolve an open question posed by Dussault and Makowsky regarding the chordal vertex division of bipartite graphs.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in various applications, but their performance is significantly hindered when dealing with datasets that have skewed class distributions. One of the primary causes of this issue is the bias introduced during training, where the model tends to favor the majority class. To address this problem, researchers have developed several techniques to adjust the decision boundary, but these methods often exacerbate the problem in incremental learning scenarios, particularly when new information is added to the model after training. In this study, we evaluate a range of calibration techniques in the context of extreme multi-class incremental learning, where datasets are characterized by skewed distributions and a large number of classes. Our findings reveal that a combination of temperature scaling and entropy minimization can effectively mitigate the bias introduced during training, even when models are trained on extremely imbalanced datasets. Notably, our proposed method outperforms existing techniques in terms of both overall accuracy and the accuracy of minority classes.

This paper presents a novel propellant-assisted bipedal locomotion system, which overcomes the power density limitations hindering current motor-driven robots. A bipedal robot is designed and tested, featuring 7 degrees of freedom and a unique hybrid actuation system. The actuation system combines pneumatic artificial muscles for actuation and a compact motor for actuator repositioning. A custom repositioning mechanism is developed to facilitate rapid and precise actuator repositioning, enabling the robot to execute continuous gait cycles. A control algorithm is implemented to synchronise the actuator repositioning with leg movement, ensuring coordinated locomotion. Experimental results demonstrate the robot's ability to walk at a speed of 0.1 m/s with a 10-second cycle time, utilising a previously established 15-second cycle time passive dynamic walker model. A power budget analysis is conducted to assess the system's power efficiency and performance.

Let K be a field and V be a valued domain with the valuation map valued in R+ towards the fraction field of V, denoted as K. The valuation is said to be complete if the residue domain, denoted as R, is equal to the set of all elements w in K such that the valuation of w is greater than or equal to 1. This paper aims to explore the properties of domain families that possess a complete residue map.

Modern CPUs are highly optimized for specific types of computations, but this optimization comes at the cost of increased power consumption. To overcome this limitation, we introduce HyperDegrade, a novel technique that intentionally degrades CPU performance by lowering clock frequencies. Our research reveals that lowering CPU clock frequencies to a small fraction of their maximum efficiency yields significant improvements in energy consumption. Specifically, we found that reducing CPU frequencies to between 10-30% of their maximum efficiency results in up to 10x energy savings. To demonstrate the effectiveness of HyperDegrade, we developed a system that automatically identifies the optimal frequency range for a given application and applies the technique to a variety of workloads, including web browsers, media players, and scientific simulations. Our technique is implemented as a simple software patch that requires no changes to the underlying application or operating system. Overall, HyperDegrade provides a simple and effective way to save energy on modern energy-constrained computing devices.

We investigate the possibility of a two-body bottom quark decay mediated by a scalar interaction to account for the discrepancy in the muon magnetic moment anomaly, considering the recent discovery of a rare process where the Higgs boson decays into two bottom squarks. By analyzing the current experimental data from the CMS collaboration, we derive constraints on the coupling between the Higgs boson and bottom quarks, finding that if the bottom squark is massless, the particle's mass must be at least 1.5 TeV. However, if we assume the scenario where the bottom quark squark has a mass of 500 GeV, the muon magnetic moment anomaly can be fully explained by the decay process, provided that the scalar-mediated bottom quark decay width is less than 0.01 picobecquerels. We also investigate the implications of this scenario on the top quark decay process and find that it can still be consistent with the current experimental data, if the scalar-mediated charm quark coupling is less than 0.01 times the Standard Model-like coupling.

A novel unknotting procedure for classical and welded links is proposed, which involves transforming a given knot or link into a trivial unknot or a trivial split split-link through the elimination of a local tangle. This process results in a trivial unknot or split link, but the resulting trivial unknot or split link is not necessarily derived from the original knot or link. It is proven that this unknotting procedure for classical knots and links is irreversible, whereas its welded unknotting counterpart is feasible. This implication is that under this method, all classical knots and links are equivalent to a trivial unknot or split link, respectively. Furthermore, this procedure is shown to be impractical for a specific non-twisted link, referred to as $L_{1,1,1,1}$, under this unknotting method. This demonstration is used to illustrate the fundamental distinction between classical and welded knots and links.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a finite type tropical arc has a finite generating set over the tropical semifield. This achievement is accompanied by a related theorem, which ensures the finite generation of the rational function semifields of a certain class of tropical varieties, semialgebraic sets, and semicanonical paths.

We demonstrate that the combination of the Fox-Hacker loop and a Vassiliev invariant of order three results in a characteristic of the same order for oriented links. Furthermore, we establish that a specific subclass of Fox-Hatcher loops is sufficient to uniquely identify oriented links. Building on this foundation, we introduce an explicit formula for determining the aforementioned combination in terms of oriented link polynomials.

Recent experiments conducted with the KATRIN apparatus have yielded a precise upper limit on how much neutrino electrons can contribute to measurements of molecular molecular electron masses. This upper limit is extremely tight, amounting to 0.83eV with 90% certainty. To obtain more specific information, researchers used data from the KATRIN experiment to calculate the minimum possible mass of the neutrino electron at 4.2eV, an estimation that is subject to uncertainty due to molecular structure. To make accurate measurements of neutrino electron masses in the future, scientists must be able to precisely measure molecular electron masses, in addition to other factors. To illustrate this point, a comparison was made between theoretical predictions and experimental data for molecular electron masses, showing a discrepancy of 0.004eV. This discrepancy suggests that a future experiment with the same sensitivity as the KATRIN apparatus would be able to establish a lower limit on the neutrino electron mass of 0.4eV. Furthermore, if an appropriate atomic clock can be developed, a future experiment with the same sensitivity as the KATRIN apparatus would be able to establish a lower limit on the neutrino electron mass of 0.0001eV.

A computação desempenha um papel fundamental na análise de imagens, com técnicas de processamento de imagens sendo amplamente utilizadas em diversas áreas, como diagnóstico médico e processamento de vídeo. Dada a complexidade de muitos algoritmos de processamento de imagens, é comum que uma única imagem exija um tempo de processamento prolongado. A presente pesquisa compara a eficiência de duas abordagens distintas para multiplicação de matrizes: uma implementação sequencial em processador e uma implementação paralela em processador gráfico. Os resultados demonstraram que a abordagem paralela oferece um desempenho significativamente melhor, com um tempo de execução cerca de dez vezes menor do que o tempo de execução sequencial.

The proposed approach is designed to address the limitations of existing methods, which often fail to account for the high cost of communication and the need for agents to collaborate in real-time. The key innovation of the proposed approach is the use of a standard network of robots, which allows agents to collaborate without the need for a central coordinator. The proposed approach is tested in a series of simulations, which demonstrate its effectiveness in a variety of scenarios, including the navigation of agents through a maze and the capture of a target in a dynamic environment. Quantum corrections to scattering processes at large distances, specifically infrared (IR) singularities, can significantly impact final state data and may provide valuable insights into the non-perturbative sector of QCD. These include phenomena such as confinement, hadronization, and energy loss. While hadronization effects are generally well-established for hadronic final states, they are less understood in cases where there is an IR singular component, such as in hadronization around a photon. To accurately describe such cases, we need to develop an understanding of the interplay between perturbative and non-perturbative physics in QCD. In this context, we have derived new results for universal, process-independent, IR corrections using T*-cuts of rescaled amplitude building blocks, and we have identified previously unexplored contributions from soft-photon exchanges between external legs. These contributions can be significant and require careful consideration. We illustrate our approach using QED calculations for hadronization corrections to $e^+e^-\to\gamma_{\rm s}$-jet events.

Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) is an emerging collaborative machine learning technique that enables multiple parties to jointly train a machine learning model without sharing their data. Researchers have proposed VFL as a privacy-preserving alternative to centralized data collection for sensitive applications such as credit scoring and medical diagnosis. In this paper, we challenge the notion that VFL inherently protects user data by presenting a novel attack called the Privacy Assault via VFL (PA-VFL) attack. This attack allows an adversary to reconstruct the original input data of a participating entity in the VFL system. Unlike previous attacks, PA-VFL does not require the adversary to control the majority of participants or have access to a majority of the model. Instead, the adversary only needs to control a small fraction of participants and a small fraction of the model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PA-VFL in a real-world VFL scenario and show that it can successfully reconstruct the original input data with high accuracy. Our findings suggest that users participating in VFL systems should be aware of the inherent risks and take additional measures to protect their data.

Nonparametric density estimation is a nonparametric method used to estimate an unknown probability density function from a given sample. This paper introduces a novel kernel estimation approach that automatically adjusts a kernel's bandwidth and kernel arguments based on the data, eliminating the need for kernel smoothing. A small set of randomly generated fourier components are used to create an approximated regression function, which is equivalent to learning the data given features. This approach is theoretically justified to converge to the true density function and is supported by both simulation and real-world data experiments.

This research presents a new approach to represent a group that acts on the Cartesian power of a set as the wreath product of the set's parent group and the set's symmetric group. We demonstrate that any group that acts on the Cartesian power of a set can be expressed as such a wreath product, using the standard action of the group on the set's parent set. This Cartesian partition method provides the smallest possible index for a subgroup of the wreath product that is equivalent to the given group. Furthermore, we present an innovative approach to address the Isomorphism Problem for groups that act on the Cartesian power of a set.

If a conformally flat hypersurface $M^n$ lies within a hypersphere of $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$, we can assign it a M\"obius curvature vector $\mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ within the M\"obius space $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$. For the M\"obius scalar curvature to reach its maximum possible value, $M^n$ must be a CM-type hypersurface, and all such hypersurfaces share the same M\"obius scalar curvature.

Automated segmentation of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images is a crucial preprocessing step in cardiac image analysis. Deep learning methods, particularly U-Net, have become the gold standard for this task. However, these methods often struggle with rare diseases and underdeveloped anatomy, especially in children. This study evaluates the performance of a pre-trained adult U-Net on six patients with complex congenital heart defects, including Tetralogy of Fallot and single ventricle defects. Cardiac MRI images are essential for surgical planning and post-surgical monitoring. Despite their importance, MRI image interpretation can be time-consuming and prone to human error. Our research indicates that the adult U-Net's performance is significantly compromised in these rare cases, with substantial increases in false positives and false negatives. Our findings suggest that using a single, general-purpose model may not be suitable for all cardiac MRI image segmentations. Instead, we propose a tailored model training approach that takes into account the anatomy of each specific patient.

The standard phase field models, which incorporate gradient terms in the free energy, become problematic when analyzing the corresponding Euler-Lagrange equations due to the unfavorable scaling of the gradient component. This issue is exacerbated by the possible loss of regularity in the model's parameters, which depend on spatial location. To tackle this challenge, we establish weak convergence results for certain deteriorating model sequences, which can be applied to derive asymptotic limits in the context of material optimization problems.

A new type of wireless system that uses SWIPT was examined in this study, which enables some devices to both receive data and recharge their batteries from a single transmission. The paper focused on an optimization problem to allocate transmission resources in order to meet specific quality of service requirements for various applications. The problem's complexity was reduced by developing a specialized algorithm to efficiently solve it. The proposed solution's effectiveness was demonstrated through numerical results.

This paper presents an all-items observing policy for the popular class of restless bandit problems, specifically those with concave reward structures. We develop a new R-approximation algorithm for optimal policies in such systems with restricted parameters. By demonstrating the exact optimality of all-items scheduling under certain conditions, our solution builds on existing work that had an gap of at most 2. Our theoretical advances enable an efficient N-K approximation for the general case and an exact optimal policy for the specific concave reward structure, offering a significant improvement in understanding and scheduling such systems.

As a condition approaches its extreme limit, the tail behavior of a conditional distribution $X|Y=y$ can significantly diverge from its unconditional counterpart $X$. This phenomenon has been observed in recent studies on very high quantiles of conditioned distributions. This paper investigates the asymptotic relationship between the tail of a Fréchet or Weibull distributed $X|Y=y$ and its unconditional Weibull or Fréchet distribution, respectively, where the conditioning variable $y$ tends towards a specific value $y_\star$. Our analysis reveals that under certain joint distribution assumptions, the tail of $X|Y=y$ exhibits a distinct divergence from its unconditional counterpart, showcasing the extreme traits of conditional models.

Resolving Word Meaning Clarification (WMC) is a crucial task in Natural Language Understanding (NLU) that addresses the ambiguity of words in NLP applications. As we move towards more complex NLP applications, such as Neural Machine Translation (NMT) and Question Answering (QA), accurately understanding word meanings becomes increasingly important. Recently, Huang et al. proposed a new evaluation metric for assessing word semantic clarity. In this study, we introduce a new evaluation dataset and employ the CLARE metric to evaluate word semantic clarity. Building upon the work of Huang et al., we developed an enhanced model called GlossBERT for WMC evaluation, which incorporates glosses from Chinese-English bilingual dictionaries to enrich word semantics. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework outperforms the baseline model CLARE, as evidenced by our improved F1 score of 0.5050 compared to the baseline's 0.4800.

Multimodal instructions are commonly used in various settings to guide individuals through complex tasks, and their importance has been widely recognized in the literature. However, there is a lack of comprehensive research on human comprehension of sequential multimodal instructions, particularly in tasks that require a combination of multiple modalities. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted an extensive study on human sequencing of sequential multimodal instructions by creating a unique dataset consisting of 1,200 annotated samples across 60 complex tasks that involve both visual and textual instructions. Our analysis of the data reveals that people often struggle to accurately sequence instructions for complex tasks, and that certain instructional components are more challenging to sequence than others. Additionally, we found that certain visual aids are more effective than others in assisting with the sequencing process. To further this line of research, our findings provide a valuable foundation for developing improved methods for creating sequential multimodal instructions.

The complex network of neuronal connections in the brain is characterized by numerous small, disconnected components that form when mapping the connectome. A critical mass of connectivity is required to trigger an action potential that propagates through the network as an electrical signal. Understanding the precise distribution of disconnected components in this network is crucial in determining the threshold at which it transitions from isolation to a single, interconnected component. In this study, a theoretical model is developed to predict the probability of forming a single, interconnected component as the probability of connection between neurons increases. The model's predictions are validated using Monte Carlo simulations and compared to real-world data from the mouse brain.

Consider $x$ as a real number and $k$ as a positive integer. Let $Q_n(x,k)$ be a sequence of polynomials in $x$ with rational coefficients and the property that all of its roots are real numbers. When $k$ is close to $2^{1/4}n^{3/4}\sqrt{Q'_n(2,n/k)}$, the following relationship holds: $Q'_n(2,n/k)/Q_n(2,n/k) = -x$. This sequence of polynomials can be referred to as the universal Airy polynomials. These polynomials can be expressed in terms of hypergeometric functions and can be used to derive various combinatorial identities. Additionally, they can be related to other classical polynomials, such as Jacobi, Meixner-Sch\"{u}rf, and Hahn polynomials.

Next-generation gravitational wave detectors will be limited by the noise generated by thermal vibrations in their optical resonators. A novel design called the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer (sSI) is proposed to overcome this limitation by reducing thermal vibration noise at high frequencies. The sSI design, which involves splitting a laser beam into two paths with different lengths, allows for a more precise measurement of thermal vibrations in the frequency range of 10 kHz to 100 kHz. This measurement can be used to improve the detection of gravitational waves in this frequency range by a factor of approximately 3 compared to traditional Michelson interferometers. The proposed sSI design is compatible with existing detector configurations and does not require any additional optical equipment.

In massive MIMO systems with random access, users are allocated to multiple access ports, and the intersection of their service areas is crucial for successful packet transmission. We investigate the phenomenon where some ports have non-intersecting service areas due to the large number of ports and small cell size. A mathematical model is developed to calculate the proportion of non-intersecting areas, and we find that this proportion increases with the number of ports and decreases with cell size. A new access control method is proposed to prevent packet transmission in non-intersecting areas.

To better understand the formation of terrestrial planets, we must first identify and characterize the substructures within protoplanetary disks. Using hydrodynamical simulations, we previously investigated how vertical shear instability creates density waves and filaments in disk midplanes. In this study, we developed a method to analyze the 2D power spectrum of simulated images, which can help observers distinguish the characteristic signatures of shear instability from other structures. We also created a database of simulated observations to predict how these features would appear in millimeter wavelengths, where dust emission is most prominent.

We have developed a new theoretical framework for describing the properties of dense nuclear matter, specifically focusing on the direct and squeezeability aspects. Our model, named Big Apple, successfully replicates experimental data on various measurable properties such as charge radii, isotope masses, and saturation properties. Furthermore, the theoretical predictions made by Big Apple are in line with the requirements of the neutron star's mass-radius relationship and the tidal deformability observed in neutron star mergers. By applying the equation of state generated by Big Apple to neutrino-driven convection in a supernova, we found that the "absolute stability condition" is a critical factor in determining the boundary between white dwarfs and neutron stars. As a result, the theoretical framework of Big Apple offers valuable insights into the behavior of neutron stars, white dwarfs, and supernovae.

Using Density Functional Theory and Dynamical Mean-Field Theory, we've studied the electronic properties of SrMnO$_3$. Our calculations show that DFT alone fails to accurately describe the material's band gap, but including atomic physics and adjusting the oxygen 2p and manganese 3d levels in DMFT yields the correct gap size. We've also used DMFT to calculate the material's spectral function and verify its experimental observations. A key issue we've identified is the discrepancy between the actual valence band maximum and the highest energy state in the DMFT-derived onsite spectrum. We've also used DMFT to investigate the $p$-$d$ hybridization in SrMnO$_3$, and our results indicate that shifting the O 2p levels relative to the Mn 3d levels significantly impacts the material's onsite spectrum.

We propose a method to create an M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate between two ions using optical fields that are not sensitive to frequency variations. This approach involves applying two types of sideband cooling, specifically red and blue, to each ion. By carefully selecting the frequencies of these fields, we can achieve a method that is robust to frequency variations, making it possible to create a high-fidelity two-qubit gate using a short pulse duration. Our research indicates that a gate infidelity of 0.002 can be achieved with a pulse duration of 0.5 microseconds when using two-frequency fields that are 2.5 times broader than a single-frequency field. This method has the potential to create a scalable quantum computing architecture that can operate with a limited number of distinct frequencies, allowing for the use of a single type of sideband cooling and two-frequency field to create an efficient and robust quantum computing system.

The structural transition in paraelectric perovskites from high to low temperatures is linked to the formation of complex, nanometer-scale disorder within the crystal lattice. This phenomenon is not fully understood, and its relationship to the material's dielectric properties remains unclear. Utilizing a combination of techniques, we have developed a new method to visualize the structural disorder in these materials. By integrating data from X-ray and neutron diffraction experiments with theoretical modeling, we have developed a structural model that accurately replicates the diffraction patterns observed. This model reveals that the disorder in these materials consists of distinct regions with different orientations of the crystal lattice, and we have determined that these regions are on the order of 10 nanometers in size. Our findings provide a new perspective on the structural disorder in perovskites and pave the way for further research into the relationship between structure and function in these materials.

Based on the Dirac-hallon model, we develop a simple yet comprehensive framework to explore strong correlations within a Dirac metal. This model incorporates a specific type of four-particle interaction, allowing us to derive a simple formula for the critical point of this interaction. This formula is applicable to various Dirac materials, including those derived from graphene, the Berker lattice, and stacked tri-layers of ABC. Our research reveals that strong interactions can lead to a superconducting state in the Dirac metals under certain conditions.

This document outlines the mathematical principles behind frequency ratios that accommodate two distinct groups of musical notes, a concept explored in the history of music theory. Notable examples of such systems include the 31-tone equal temperament developed by Erhard Friedrich Schmidt, various quarter-tone scales, and the 24-tone scale of Indian classical music. We have established a general theoretical framework for evaluating and comparing these systems based on their ability to accurately represent complex frequency relationships, and we have applied this framework to evaluate specific well-known systems. Furthermore, we have established a connection between this framework and the field of psychophysics, suggesting that it could be utilized to select an optimal musical frequency system through human perception.

We examine the potential of the NA62 experiment to detect a new neutral lepton species, 'N', in $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decays, within a specific mass range of 150-550 MeV/c$^2$. Our study utilizes the anticipated 10 fb$^{-1}$ dataset from Phase II of the experiment. We predict 10-100 observable events for 'N' with masses between 150-400 MeV/c$^2$, given that 'N' has a lifetime exceeding 100 meters. Our findings also suggest that the experiment can determine the lifetime of 'N' with a precision of 0.5-2 orders of magnitude within this mass range. Furthermore, we explore the potential for identifying the decay of 'N' into neutrinos, which could provide insights into the Lorentz-violating operator responsible for its production.

This study delves into the impact of a rotating Sagnac interferometer on spectral changes, particularly in relation to a rotating reference frame. By applying a 180-degree rotation to the interferometer's polarization axis, we can identify specific frequency shifts that occur within certain spectral ranges. The study also explores how these spectral shifts are influenced by the rotation's angular velocity and the size of the area enclosed by the light path, taking into account the acceleration experienced by an accelerating system in a rotating Galilean frame. The research aims to provide a deeper understanding of how spectral changes can be used to measure angular velocity and polarization axis rotation in a rotating Sagnac interferometer.

We introduce and study the parabolic adjoint operation, denoted as $\alpha^\vee$, which maps a parabolic root $\alpha$ to another parabolic root. We establish key properties of this operation, including the fact that for any simple parabolic root $\alpha$, its corresponding Weyl group element $s_\alpha$ preserves the set of parabolic roots, and the parabolic Weyl group can be viewed as a subgroup of the full Weyl group under this action. This allows us to define the notion of connected components for nilvarieties, specifically for $e\mathcal{N}_\lambda$ in type $A$. We also develop the concept of Weierstrass segments and show that the connected components of $e\mathcal{N}_\lambda$ can be represented as $\mathcal{O}_{\mu_1}\cup\dots\cup\mathcal{O}_{\mu_r}$, where each $\mu_i$ corresponds to a distinct Weierstrass segment. This result is then applied to describe the $G$-orbits of the Springer resolution in type $A$.

A recent breakthrough in neural language modeling has seen significant success with the transformer architecture. However, for smaller model sizes, simpler models like $n$-gram have consistently outperformed them. This paper presents a straightforward yet effective method of combining these two approaches by using a neural network to enhance the $n$-gram model. Through a series of experiments, we found that this method of pretraining on $n$-gram data before fine-tuning on task-specific datasets yields superior results compared to training neural models from scratch. Notably, this approach also surpasses the use of pre-trained corpora in certain scenarios. Furthermore, we discovered that simply adding a residual learning module to the existing $n$-gram model results in significant performance gains.

We establish a connection between non-toric toric 3-folds $X_\tau$ and the space of non-toric toric 3-folds, by demonstrating that $X_\tau$ can be transformed into a family of Calabi-Yau hypersurfaces within a twisted product of $\mathbb{P}^2$'s, through a specific type of geometric modification. This is achieved by either shrinking a $\mathbb{P}^1$ in a linear system of $\mathbb{P}^2$'s or by applying a Atiyah flop to a $\mathbb{P}^1$ in a linear system of ample divisors. Consequently, we obtain a family of $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties over $\mathbb{C}[t]$, whose generic fiber is a smooth hypersurface in the twisted product of $\mathbb{P}^2$'s, and whose special fiber is isomorphic to $X_\tau$. This result is applicable to a broader class of toric varieties, specifically those that are smooth and complete.

This paper introduces a novel 3D dense face reconstruction and face alignment framework, known as SADRNet, which uniquely employs a dual network structure. SADRNet's self-aligned dual network design, comprising self-supervised alignment and reconstruction components, enables a unique dual task execution. The alignment and reconstruction modules are trained in a mutually reinforcing manner, with the dual network structure allowing for mutual supervision and mutual benefit. This innovative approach overcomes the limitations of conventional single network models, which often struggle with mutual supervision and mutual benefit. SADRNet's self-supervised training mechanism, on the other hand, enables the dual network to achieve mutual alignment and alignment accuracy improvements. The SADRNet framework's self-supervised dual network structure, therefore, enables the model to achieve superior face alignment and reconstruction performance. We develop a spontaneous symmetry breaking framework for fracton models, analogous to the Higgs mechanism, and derive simplified Gaussian models from interacting systems that exhibit this phenomenon. By applying this technique, we obtain spontaneous symmetry breaking models for the X-cube and three-dimensional elastic models, enabling the derivation of Majorana elastic modes within these systems.

A significant density fluctuation in the early universe's early stages could have led to the formation of primordial black holes. To create these, the stages of an inflationary period followed by a period of cold inflationary expansion must be considered. In this study, we investigate the possibility of forming primordial black holes after an inflationary period driven by an $\alpha$-attractor model, where we assume that the disruption of a secondary field's vacuum, caused by the sudden change in Hubble's rate during the transition, could generate the necessary fluctuations. In order to achieve a sufficient level of fluctuations to create a sufficient number of primordial black holes, we require a period of inflation lasting at least 60 Hubble times, which is consistent with the constraints imposed by the CMB's observations. We then use a semi-classical approach to calculate the primordial black holes' mass spectrum, and we find that a sufficiently large number of them could be produced with a mass range that could be detected by future gravitational wave observatories like LISA, LIGO, and the Einstein Telescope.

Given a labeled tree, we've identified the deepest nodes at each level and analyzed various properties of these nodes in different types of trees, including binary, ordered, and labeled trees. We've also derived the generating function for the number of ways to place weighted labels on a tree so that its deepest vertices form a specific subgraph. Additionally, we've determined the average weight of these functions and investigated how they change with the weight, focusing on scenarios where the weight is either very low or very high.

Informed OCR (iOCR) is an Informed OCR tool that utilizes Informed CT (certain context) to enhance traditional optical character recognition (OCR) technology. In recent years, the widespread adoption of electronic voting systems has been accompanied by concerns regarding their security. Although several nations have implemented electronic voting machines, paper-based ballot marking systems remain the most secure voting method. To balance ballot security and accessibility, we developed iOCR to assist non-disabled voters in accurately reviewing paper ballots. We tested iOCR against conventional OCR technologies, including Tesseract, and the results showed that iOCR outperformed them, achieving a total accuracy of 99.9% when processing election ballot totals.

A linear regression model that incorporates temporal dependencies is widely used in various fields, such as econometrics and engineering, to forecast future outcomes. Typically, this model is expressed in a non-linear form, making theoretical analysis difficult. This study aims to examine a linear version of the temporal regression model with Gaussian noise, where the model's parameters are significantly greater than the available sample size. By utilizing a non-asymptotic risk bound, we can conclude that a high-risk, over-parameterized temporal linear model nonetheless produces predictions that are statistically similar to those of a well-estimated, independent Gaussian linear model.

Speech enhancement is a crucial application in audio signal processing, with the development of deep learning models being particularly significant. In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning framework that utilizes attention mechanisms to effectively enhance speech quality. The attention mechanism allows the model to focus on relevant information and disregard background noise, which is achieved through two attention modules that extract features and enhance speech quality, respectively. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over other attention-based models and a wide range of baseline models. Furthermore, our proposed framework is unique in that it is the first to utilize attention mechanisms in a bidirectional manner for speech enhancement.

This research paper delves into the potential risks of using popular music to disseminate harmful pathogens covertly. We outline a possible strategy for executing this plan, which involves modifying music with microscopic pathogens and distributing the altered music through online platforms and social media. However, we believe that human curiosity and our innate desire to explore new experiences will ultimately thwart this scheme. Our analysis suggests that this plan is unlikely to succeed due to the fact that people are more inclined to engage with music that does not pose a threat to their well-being.

In decentralized energy markets, users can autonomously manage their energy usage by engaging in peer-to-peer transactions. However, limited information and unpredictable market conditions can hinder optimal decision-making. To address this challenge, we propose a cautious self-planning approach that leverages scenario-based optimization and value functions to maximize the storage device's value. By incorporating scenario-based optimization, the approach allows the storage device to make informed decisions based on a range of possible future conditions. Additionally, the use of value functions enables the device to learn from past experiences and make better decisions in new situations. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate that our approach can effectively manage storage devices in dynamic, information-limited environments.

The ultra-fast movement of electrons within atoms and molecules can significantly alter their chemical properties and structural stability. To effectively control light-matter interactions at an electronic level, researchers need a deeper understanding of electron movement within atoms and molecules. This study utilizes a combination of high-energy X-ray and attosecond light pulses to examine the ultra-fast electron movement within carbon monoxide. By firing an X-ray photon at the molecule, it causes the ejection of a C1s core electron, which in turn triggers an even more rapid Auger electron, resulting in the formation of a He-like CO molecule with two valence electrons in motion. To better understand this process, theoretical models were employed to interpret experimental data, ultimately revealing that multiple electron movement patterns coexist within the molecule.

The study examined the effects of rotation and turbulence on a simplified Earth model, where the atmosphere was treated as a thickened shell with a unique set of physical properties. The study found that the atmosphere's rotation rate and the presence of turbulence significantly influenced circulation patterns, with the atmosphere transitioning from geostrophic to cyclostrophic regimes as the rotation rate decreased. The study also found that turbulence had a more pronounced effect on circulation patterns in the presence of weak rotation, with increased turbulence leading to more efficient heat distribution and a decrease in the atmosphere's rotation rate. Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in various computer vision tasks, particularly when combined with large-scale supervised learning. However, most of these models are designed for one-time training and training that takes place in batches. In contrast, continuous learning, which involves training a model in an ongoing stream of data, is essential for many real-world computer vision applications. Unfortunately, typical DNNs suffer from catastrophic forgetting when subjected to sequential batch learning. This paper presents a new approach to batch learning from large data streams that enables the model to learn new information while retaining previously learned information without requiring modifications to the model's architecture. This method is demonstrated on a large-scale dataset of one million classes from the ImageNet-1M, where the proposed approach is compared to alternative methods such as regularized and replay-based approaches. The results show that the proposed method outperforms these methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

This paper provides novel analytical and geometrical perspectives on the concept of algebraic multiplicity within linear algebra, offering fresh insights into its complex nature. A key formula is derived to express the algebraic multiplicity of an eigenvalue in terms of a companion invariant, which in turn is defined by the rank of a matrix constructed from the linear operator. Additionally, this derivation yields new inequalities related to the outer and inner spectral radii of a given operator. The study also incorporates geometrical applications, particularly in the context of the spectral theory of a class of differential operators. A specific companion invariant is defined for a class of non-self-adjoint operators, and a formula is established to express the algebraic multiplicity of a point spectrum element of such an operator. The algebraic multiplicity of such an operator is determined by the index of a specific projection associated with that spectrum point. The proposed index is shown to be invariant under continuous deformations of a class of operator families, and this invariance is demonstrated in the context of a string quartet. A quantum-assisted optical phase measurement technique is proposed, utilizing a pair of D-doped silicon crystals as the sensing system. This approach takes advantage of a unique property of these qubits, where their long-lived dipoles allow for stable coherence over extended periods. A theoretical model is developed, incorporating optical coupling to a microwave cavity, and it is shown that the system can generate bosonic pairs and squeezing due to an unusual interaction. This process is further enhanced by the coherent driving of the cavity. As a result, a highly entangled state is created, which is ideal for optical phase assessment. Notably, this method is not limited to this specific system and can be applied to any qubits with long-lived dipoles.

This study presents a complete configuration interaction analysis of the ground state spin doublet and excited states in a pair of exchange-coupled electron donors in silicon, considering all six valleys. Utilizing a CM model based on an effective mass approximation that accounts for all six valleys, we calculated the energy levels and wave functions for various states. Comparing our results to spin-orbit coupled calculations, our calculations accurately reproduce the energy levels and wave functions for both shallow and deep well cases. Our calculations also show that the inter-valley coupling has a greater impact on the excited states than on the ground state. Furthermore, our calculations show that the inter-valley coupling significantly affects the energy splitting of the excited S-states, with the nearest excited state with L=2 symmetry being split into two distinct energy levels.

Researchers have been studying the quantum Hall effect in mercury telluride quantum wells, specifically those adjacent to the gapless L-band, for an extended period. In this study, we utilized a theoretical approach to analyze quantum conduction in quantum wells made of mercury telluride. Our analysis was based on the Dirac equation, taking into account the material's symmetry and boundary conditions. We discovered that a quantum well adjacent to a gapless L-band exhibits a unique property where the quantum conduction of particles described by the Dirac equation is quantized in units of e^2/h, in contrast to electrons within the L-band whose conduction is quantized in units of e^2/2h. Furthermore, our study demonstrated that a specific pattern of mercury telluride layers can create a quantum well with a sizable gap, allowing for the observation of 2e^2/h quantum conduction.

This paper evaluates a novel adaptive collaborative non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) protocol's performance, particularly in low-speed urban driving scenarios. In these scenarios, signal interference cancellation (SIC) failure is prevalent in traditional time-domain NOMA (TD-NOMA) systems, compromising their reliability. The defective SIC failures can be rectified through signal exchange between TD-NOMA users, effectively transforming them into a hybrid power-domain and time-domain NOMA (CP-TD-NOMA) configuration. The collaborative CP-TD-NOMA (CC-NOMA) protocol is designed to dynamically adapt to changing channel conditions and user demands, optimizing overall system performance. Analytical expressions for outage probabilities and average sum rates are derived for the CC-NOMA protocol, and Monte Carlo simulations validate these expressions' accuracy. The simulation results demonstrate that the CC-NOMA protocol outperforms both traditional TD-NOMA and the basic CP-TD-NOMA (CC-NOMA) protocol in terms of average sum rates, particularly in scenarios with high defective SIC failure rates. The CC-NOMA protocol's performance gains are attributed to its ability to efficiently utilize both time and frequency resources, thereby increasing overall system capacity. The proposed protocol is especially beneficial in scenarios with high defective SIC failure rates, where it can achieve up to a 20% increase in average sum rates compared to the traditional TD-NOMA protocol. The use of Dynamic Time Division Duplexing (TDD) has become an effective technique for enhancing spectral efficiency in fifth-generation (5G) wireless networks. By adjusting TDD configurations in real-time, it is possible to adapt to changing traffic demands and minimize scheduling overhead. This paper presents a novel scheduling method for Distributed TDD systems that leverages the adjustment of TDD configurations. The proposed scheduling approach is modeled using a discrete-time stochastic game, which takes into account the statistical behavior of the system. The proposed method is evaluated through simulations, which demonstrate significant improvements in spectral efficiency and successful convergence to an equilibrium solution.

Using the Cuntz-Nakamura polynomial mapping, we have analyzed the asymptotic behavior of normalized static correlations in the 3D Ising model on a lattice of size $L^3$, where $L$ is odd, as it grows larger. By applying the Hossain-Nakamura theorem, we derived an exact formula for the third-order magnetization cumulant $c_3$, which is expressed as the fixed point value of a dynamical system. We then compared this theoretical value with Monte Carlo simulation data and found a close match. Additionally, we derived an upper bound for the first-order cumulant $c_1$ and obtained numerical estimates for cumulant values $c_k$ for $k$ ranging from 4 to 10.
