This project proposes a novel 3D location recognition network based on deep learning, called AttDLNet, which utilizes a LiDAR sensor to collect data. To enhance efficiency and reduce computational complexity, the network selectively focuses on relevant areas using an attention mechanism, thereby discarding unnecessary data. Specifically, an attention module is employed to identify and remove redundant points from the LiDAR point cloud, while a series of fully connected layers extract features from the remaining data. To obtain a comprehensive 3D image, a series of 2D images are created by projecting the point cloud onto a grid, and a series of location recognition fully connected layers are used to determine the location. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed network outperforms existing methods, achieving a location recognition accuracy of 90.5% and a forward/backward recognition accuracy of 98.2%.

The rising demand for streaming services has compelled organizations to invest in high-speed networks and servers capable of delivering top-notch video quality. However, delivering multiple video quality options to a large audience can be costly. To reduce expenses, transcoding is often outsourced to third-party cloud service providers. This study evaluates the performance of an Hadoop-based video transcoding system, taking into account various cloud configurations and their impact on throughput, latency, and cost. By simulating this system using an open-source tool, we found that a cloud environment with a mix of server types can offer better cost efficiency without compromising performance.

This study examines the impact of temperature on the screening process in doped graphene, specifically how it varies with changes in temperature and carrier density. We utilize a non-local, temperature-dependent screening model to calculate the heat capacity of doped graphene across a broad temperature range, from 4K to 300K. Our results indicate that the screening process in doped graphene is highly non-local and becomes increasingly so as temperature rises. We also find that the temperature-dependent screening process has a notable effect on the specific heat of doped graphene, with the model's calculations showing a significant deviation from the predictions made by a local, fixed-screening model. Ultimately, our research highlights the importance of accounting for the non-local and temperature-dependent screening process when analyzing the physical properties of doped graphene.

Continuous dialogue synthesis in a changing conversational environment is
challenging for current speech systems. To overcome this difficulty, a new method
is proposed, called MaskedDialogue, which uses a masking technique to generate
context-aware speech. This technique masks parts of the input sentence and trains
a model to predict the missing information using input and output context. As a
result, the model can generate natural sentences that fit the input context.
Experiments show that MaskedDialogue outperforms other models, including
traditional sequence-to-sequence models and attention-based ones, in producing
high-quality sentences that fit the input context.

We examine the influence of a specific trap on a Klein-Gordon model, where the anharmonic oscillator has two types of behaviors - one that dissipates energy and another that amplifies it. We investigate how these effects impact the stability of solitary wave solutions. Our analysis reveals that energy-dissipating nonlinearity causes both types of stability to break down, whereas trap-induced superlinear but energy-conserving nonlinearity preserves both. Finally, we explore how varying strengths of both types of nonlinearity affect both modes of stability.

Q-ball studies in the context of the early universe are being expanded to include two-dimensional structures and three-dimensional structures that may form within Q-balls. These new formations, which are being examined in scalar field theories with symmetry breaking, are being compared to their BPS counterparts found in supersymmetric quantum field theories. Additionally, research is being conducted on how these objects may interact with gravitational waves and primordial black holes, which could potentially lead to observable effects in the early universe.

We investigate a specific setup in one loop quantum cosmology where a three-dimensional bulk universe with a closed spatial geometry is paired with a simply connected foliation of causal surfaces, and the boundary conditions are described by the holographic principle. The entropy of this system is linked to the geometric properties of the surfaces, and the matter content of the bulk universe is determined by the changes in these surfaces' areas, curvature, and extrinsic curvature across the foliation. The study reveals that this model generates a cyclic universe with a non-zero average size for the universe and produces a specific form of matter that can be classified as holographic dark matter, exhibiting characteristics of both type II and type III matter, and serving as a quantum counterpart to the dark sector in the $\Lambda$CDM model. The research also highlights the potential for this hCCL model to be consistent with the observed matter in the universe, and the possibility of it being a viable alternative to the standard inflationary universe model.

Given a graph G with n vertices and an associated Hermitian matrix, this paper explores the relationship between the scattering matrix and the graph's Laplacian matrix. It has been established that the (i,j)-th element of the scattering matrix corresponds to 2π times the residue of the Green's function at a specific pole, which is 0 if vertices i and j are not connected, or the negative square root of a pole located between -4 and 0 if they are connected. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the Rayleigh ratio at 0 equals the sum of the graph's open traceless poles, and the negative of this ratio is equivalent to the sum of these poles weighted by their respective multiplicities.

We explore the applicability of Leopoldt's fundamental theorem beyond commutative extensions of the rational numbers, specifically focusing on non-commutative extensions. By leveraging established results and presenting novel contributions, we establish conditions under which the Leopoldt property is preserved across certain types of non-commutative extensions, including those derived from a p-adic splitting criterion. We also generalize the original Leopoldt theorem for cyclot extensions of the rational numbers to a broader class of extensions.

We explore the connection between how often an axion-like particle appears in certain types of $B$ meson decays and the ability of current experiments to detect them. Our analysis focuses on two types of decays, where an $B$ meson turns into two other particles and an axion-like particle, or just one particle and the axion-like particle, with the axion-like particle appearing in a range of energies. We compare theoretical predictions for these scenarios with actual data from the Belle and Belle II experiments. Our findings show that existing data can limit how often these particles appear in the first type of decays, but not in the second type. However, future experiments with more accurate detection can use data from both types of decays to set limits on these particles. We also examine the potential for these particles to be discovered in certain types of decays in the future.

Identifying how language evolves in meaning is a significant issue with significant implications for various fields, including lexicography, information retrieval, and word sense disambiguation. To accomplish this task, researchers have developed methods that involve comparing linguistic data across time, often using corpora representing different periods. These methods, however, are hindered by the need for specialized, manually annotated datasets and the associated contextual information, which are costly to create. An alternative approach is to automatically generate temporal language models from diverse contextualized language frameworks, such as BERT, which can then be used to analyze semantic change. This paper reviews the current state of contextualized language framework-based change detection methods, discusses the associated challenges, and proposes a set of best practices for future studies.

The formation of massive quasar binaries is influenced by the presence of ultralight scalar bosons, which can be analyzed through the spins of their components. Researchers have previously explored the relationship between quasar binaries and these particles, but a more comprehensive understanding is required. In this study, we examine the spins of massive quasar binaries and their implications for detecting ultralight scalar bosons. Our analysis of 11 quasar binaries with masses greater than $10^9$ solar masses reveals that their spin orientations are not randomly distributed, which contradicts the expected behavior if ultralight bosons were present. This discrepancy is further exacerbated by the fact that the spins of these quasar binaries are correlated with their masses, which is inconsistent with general relativity predictions. As a result, our findings suggest that the presence of ultralight scalar bosons may be influencing the formation of massive quasar binaries in unexpected ways.

A key aspect of vertebrate neurogenesis is when neural progenitors in the retina undergo random horizontal shifts before dividing. In zebrafish retinogenesis, vertical movement of nuclei is also observed. This movement is more noticeable in certain areas of the retina, particularly in the temporal region, where nuclei move at a rate of 0.5-1.5 µm per minute. This movement is not observed in other regions of the retina. Studies have shown that blocking actomyosin contractility or altering microtubule dynamics can impede vertical movement, but blocking dynein motor activity has no effect. This suggests that forces acting on the nuclear envelope are balanced. Furthermore, blocking gap junctions has no effect on nuclei movement, suggesting that movement is not caused by the propagation of cytoplasmic currents. This study proposes that the cytoplasmic flow of nuclei is a result of the diffusion of small molecules within the retinal space. This is supported by the observation that the movement of nuclei is influenced by the size of the retinal space. This study suggests that the interkinetic nuclear movement of retinal progenitors is the result of the diffusion of small molecules within the retinal space.

This paper offers an enhanced approach to code optimization, which is crucial for techniques such as color image demosaicing and compressive video search. We introduce a novel code improvement method, which is based on a dual optimization framework that balances two objectives: maximizing the data recovery rate and minimizing the number of errors in the maximum likelihood estimation. The proposed solution is formulated as a challenging combinatorial problem, which is then addressed using a bi-level optimization framework. We develop an iterative algorithm to generate an optimal code with a fixed encoder, which is characterized by a linear system of equations. The code enhancement method is demonstrated to be effective through the application of a single optimization step, which yields significant improvements in data recovery rates. The proposed method is also shown to outperform existing code optimization strategies through the results of comparative experiments.

This research extends previous findings by Keller and Vachon regarding the long-term behavior of a specific type of fluid model that includes random obstacles. Initially, Keller and Vachon demonstrated that for a two-dimensional domain, the model's energy dissipation rate converges to a specific value with nearly optimal precision. This research, however, provides a corresponding result for higher-dimensional spaces of up to five dimensions with a slightly less precise precision, and for one-dimensional spaces, it offers an exponential rate of convergence. Furthermore, this research includes the necessary conditions for the movement of the fluid and a specific technique to generate the required fluid movement.

To enhance research productivity, research institutions often collaborate with other institutions through academic partnerships. These partnerships are essentially a type of multi-node network where institutions are interconnected. The establishment of such partnerships is influenced by a combination of rational and emotional factors, and their effectiveness is crucial for achieving shared goals. However, traditional evaluation methods primarily focus on quantitative metrics, neglecting the underlying motivations behind these partnerships. To address this shortcoming, we propose a new approach that integrates network dynamics to assess the efficacy of academic partnerships. This approach is applied to a real-world dataset of 1.2 million patents from 100 Chinese universities to demonstrate its efficacy. Furthermore, we introduce an innovative concept called the "growth rate of partnership value" to supplement existing evaluation methods. This concept is used to optimize the parameters of the evaluation model and provides a more comprehensive assessment of the partnerships' efficacy. The results of this approach are compared to existing evaluation methods, and it is found to be more accurate in predicting the future value of partnerships. Additionally, the approach is used to identify universities with high potential for partnership growth and to provide insights into the underlying factors that influence partnership success.

Research into transition metal chalcogenides, particularly NiMoP2S6, has revealed a unique state known as the pseudogap, which appears around the Fermi level without a charge density wave or Mott insulator. This study proposes that the pseudogap is caused by an extraordinary van Hove singularity, which can be created by altering the lattice structure. Researchers have modeled this compound and found that its electronic properties, including the pseudogap, are influenced by the ratio of two types of d-orbitals. By adjusting this ratio, they found that the pseudogap closes, indicating that this phenomenon is directly related to the position of these orbitals relative to the Fermi level. This study suggests that this mechanism may be at play in other compounds that exhibit the pseudogap, such as MoIrP2S6 and MoPtP2S6.

A novel spallation neutron examination device is introduced, which is being used in the Aberdeen Tunnel laboratory in Aberdeen, Scotland. The device is being used to study the characteristics of spallation neutrons produced by a 100 MeV proton beam from the Aberdeen Tandem Accelerator. The device is being used to investigate the neutron energy distribution by measuring neutron time-of-flight. The device is also being used to examine the neutron velocity distribution by measuring the angle of recoil protons from a hydrogen-rich target. The device is described in detail, and the results obtained so far are presented.

This paper investigates the ground state solutions of a biharmonic Choquard equation, specifically:
$(-\Delta)^s u(\cdot) + \lambda u(\cdot) - \left(\lambda_2 \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |u(y)|^{\mu} e^{\beta t_k |u(y)|^{\mu}}dy\right) \frac{k_s(|u(\cdot)|^{\mu}) t_k(\beta k_s^{-1}\star_{\mu} |u|^\mu)^{\wedge}}{k_s^{-1}\star_{\mu} |u|^\mu} = 0.$
Here, $0<s<1$, $\lambda, \lambda_2, \beta, k_s > 0$, and $T_k$ denotes the Trudinger-Moser nonlinearity. By applying variational methods, we prove the existence of ground state solutions under specific conditions for the parameter $\beta$.

The TESS mission is uniquely positioned to identify thousands of prime targets for the Keck telescopes to perform high-precision radial velocity measurements, which can reveal the presence of small planets. To maximize the effectiveness of this synergy, a comprehensive strategy is necessary to select the optimal sample of stars that will yield the most significant scientific discoveries. This strategy involves considering multiple factors, including the number of planets TESS can detect directly, the likelihood of finding small planets through radial velocity, the ability to characterize the stars' properties, and the diversity of stellar types. A mathematical framework is established to quantify the expected outcomes of any given sample, and a set of constraints is defined to explore various selection criteria. Ultimately, the ideal sample is determined by balancing these factors, and the results are presented in the context of different observing timeframes and the availability of additional missions like PLATO. Furthermore, the framework is applied to the TESS-Keck Examination, and the optimal sample is selected, with the expected results compared to existing and future surveys.

Indonesia is a nation with a significant population of over 270 million people, where the lack of transparency in government operations is a pressing issue. One proposed solution is to develop an automated system that can extract information from Indonesian ID cards, which contain essential personal information about the cardholder. This study presents a system that can extract data from Indonesian ID cards using optical character recognition (OCR) and natural language processing, with the goal of creating a transparent and efficient system that can be used to verify the identity of individuals. The system was tested on 100 ID cards, with a success rate of 90%, demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately extracting personal information from the cards. This research has important implications for promoting accountability and transparency in government operations, as well as for improving the efficiency of ID verification processes.

A quantum harmonic oscillator's imaginary time path integral was numerically calculated in the presence of an external force, with its ground state energy and first excited state energy examined under various conditions. These conditions included different frequencies, strengths of the applied force, and scaling parameters, and for certain conditions, the excitation gap was found to agree with theoretical predictions, while for other conditions, it deviated significantly.

This study aims to refine the rotation velocity of three asteroids - 1992 SK, Toro, and Geographos - by leveraging light curve data from previous studies and adding specific physical parameters such as size, albedo, and shape. By applying the YORP effect theory, a mathematical model was used to calculate the rate of change in the asteroids' rotation velocities. The results indicate that the YORP effect significantly impacts these asteroids, with the effect being most pronounced on 1992 SK. Furthermore, the study predicts that 1992 SK may experience a rotation velocity reversal within the next 10 million years, while Toro and Geographos are expected to do so in approximately 1.5 million years and 1.2 million years, respectively.

Social media platforms have become a primary means of communication and information dissemination, significantly impacting political discourse. This study leverages network science to analyze the dynamics of political conversations on Instagram, using the hashtag #M4A as a case study. By extracting conversation threads from the dataset, we develop a dual-layer network model to capture the relationships between users and posts. Our analysis reveals that the subgraph of active participants in the conversation exhibits a scale-free structure, with a high degree of clustering. We also identify three primary patterns of information propagation within the conversation, with the first pattern being the most frequent. Furthermore, our findings indicate that new participants tend to connect to the periphery of the network, with the degree distribution of new participants being more uniform. This study provides valuable insights into the nature of political conversations on social media platforms and highlights the potential of network science in analyzing such complex systems.

We demonstrate that the group of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of a closed surface that compactify, when considered for more than one such element, is not equivalent to the Kolmogorov ultrafilter. This applies to the broader category of compact, orientable surfaces. Additionally, we prove that certain subgroups within this category also exhibit non-Roelcke precompactness, including the geodesic flow on specific three-dimensional manifolds. This discovery brings us closer to confirming the conjecture that the flow's precompactness is also non-Roelcke.

Low-mass stars are the primary targets for studying stellar evolution and have unique characteristics, such as prolonged main sequence lifetimes and frequent close encounters with other stars. However, studying these stars is challenging due to the scarcity of well-characterized samples, especially for field stars. To address this, researchers compiled a comprehensive list of L and T dwarf candidates, applying strict criteria to ensure the samples' reliability. The resulting dataset, which includes 147 stars, was used to establish typical values for physical properties like effective temperature, surface gravity, and luminosity. The typical values for these properties were established, and the dataset was found to be suitable for use in establishing relationships between spectral features and physical properties, as well as for studying the properties of exoplanets orbiting these stars. The study also identified the most common types of low-mass stars in the field, with M5 dwarfs being the most common, and the dataset was found to be consistent with previous studies on the properties of these stars. The research also established the typical values for the properties of L and T dwarfs, and the dataset was found to be suitable for studying the properties of exoplanets orbiting these stars. Two-dimensional photonic crystals can be used to create line defects that guide light, but this approach is limited by high propagation losses and the inability to control the direction of transmission. In this study, we propose an alternative approach using a novel type of structure called a dual metastructure, which consists of two layers of asymmetric resonators. By coupling these layers through a shared surface, we can excite a type of wave called a line plasmon, which is confined to the structure and exhibits strong directionality. We demonstrate that this approach offers significant improvements over traditional photonic crystal waveguides, with up to a 10-fold increase in transmission and enhanced field confinement. The properties of this novel structure can be further optimized by adjusting the geometry of the resonators, with implications for the design of high-performance photonic devices.

The complexity of evaluating non-self-join queries is well-established, but for queries involving self-joins, only general categories have been comprehensively analyzed. This study provides a detailed complexity breakdown for every possible single-table self-join query variant and examines the impact of additional constraints such as keys, functional dependencies, and union-closed closures on evaluating these queries.

This paper explores the creation of new regular operations on infinite strings that are not regularly based, by defining two specific methods - the prefix reversal and the longest common prefix-based concatenation - and providing their definitions through a more general class of rational transformations. Additionally, we establish properties of these methods and their connections to other rational transformations, and a method to generate an infinite variety of reversal-like operations classified as weakly regular transformations.

The standard model predictions for non-resonant $B \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ decays are calculated using both perturbative and non-perturbative QCD methods, with results from light-cone effective Hamiltonian theory and factorization approach being compared. For these decays, estimated branching fractions are approximately $1.5 \times 10^{-8}$ based on QCDF and $1.3 \times 10^{-8}$ based on BL, although isospin symmetry violations affect the former's accuracy. The predicted total cross-section for $B \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ decays is estimated to be around $1.5$ picobarns, although a lower bound of $0.2$ picobarns is derived from LHCb data. The predicted branching fraction for $B \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ decays is estimated to be between $2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ and $3.3 \times 10^{-4}$, although a lower bound of $6.7 \times 10^{-5}$ is derived from the same data. The primary issue in evaluating recommender systems is the difficulty of assessing their performance on new items that have not been previously rated. This problem is particularly pronounced when recommender systems are used for sequential recommendation on streaming platforms, where new content is continuously introduced. In this paper, we tackle this challenge by devising a novel evaluation framework for predicting the sequence of content interactions with new first items. This framework is inspired by the concept of "unseen absorbing Markov chains" and is evaluated through a case study on the Netflix dataset. Our research reveals that recommending new first items based on user-user collaborative filtering can enhance the recommender's ability to predict future interactions with new content. Furthermore, we propose a metric called "unseen coexisting pullers" to quantify the recommender's susceptibility to being influenced by new first items.

This study develops estimation methods for a regression model's average absolute deviation from the median, specifically focusing on obtaining a consistent estimator of the average deviation. A new efficient estimator is proposed using a local polynomial method for a regression regressor, yielding improved performance in efficient GMM and local polynomial regression settings. Theoretical justification and numerical simulations validate the proposed method's reliability and effectiveness.

To optimize wireless communication systems affected by interference, we've developed a second-order approach that utilizes a specific type of variational equation, incorporating the Cauchy-type Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs framework. This approach enables us to determine the optimal strategy for both system design and interference management, ultimately leading to the most efficient system performance.

Dynamic systems, such as the human brain, are intricately interconnected networks that process complex information.  Deep learning models, particularly those utilizing recurrent neural networks, have achieved remarkable success in processing temporal data.  However, many successful applications of RNNs are limited to specific tasks and lack the ability to generalize.  To address this shortcoming, we propose a new type of neural network architecture, called MARRN, which combines modulated activations with an efficient representation of spatial and temporal patterns.  MARRNs are capable of generating a wide range of modulated firing patterns and are limited by only three parameters per neuron.  These networks are highly versatile and can be trained on diverse datasets, including visual object recognition and scene understanding, using a single training method.  Our research shows that MARRNs have a high level of similarity to the structural organization of the primate visual cortex and are significantly more accurate than traditional RNN baselines in visual object recognition and scene understanding tasks.

Research into the brain's ventral temporal cortex has revealed a category known as "animacy," which divides stimuli into animate beings and non-animate entities. However, the underlying nature of animacy remains unclear. We propose that animacy is not a singular entity but rather a composite of multiple features, including physical characteristics, social relevance, and cognitive processes. We argue that these components are interconnected and that their relationships can be mapped onto a geometric framework to better understand animacy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this framework can be applied to both existing and new stimuli, suggesting that animacy is a complex and multifaceted concept that is shaped by both innate and learned factors.

This research effectively accelerates the verification of quantum unique ergodicity for Dirichlet L-functions at the zero location $\frac{1}{2}+it_0$ for a substantial number of primes $p$, and also hastens the testing of Sato-Tate distribution and QUE for normalized Hecke-Maass newforms within the functional field of an elliptic curve's L-function for numerous twists, all within sub-exponential time frames. These procedures, initially proposed by Turnage-Butterley and Zudilin, are refined to yield more streamlined and user-friendly implementations, and for specific instances, are shown to be feasible with current computational resources.

We have developed a quantum relational Hoare calculus that takes into account expectations, building on an existing classical counterpart. This calculus enables the verification of programs' expectations and can demonstrate that the amount of quantum memory used by two programs is equivalent. We have also provided a corresponding axiomatic system and proved its correctness, as well as applied it to prove the correctness of key quantum programs, including early exit and teleportation.

The transmission of infectious diseases often hinges on a small group of highly active individuals known as super-spreaders. To better understand and mitigate their significant effect, identifying and isolating super-spreaders is crucial. This study explores the impact of removing one highly active node from networks representing susceptible-infected networks. We investigate various network configurations by altering network size, infection rate, and node degree distribution. Our research reveals that the removal of a single super-spreader can significantly alter the network's component structure, with the size of the largest component decreasing by up to 100%. Notably, the effect of removing a super-spreader is most pronounced in networks with high average degrees and low variance, with little impact observed in smaller networks.

Let $X$ be a complex topological vector space. This research extends the concepts of scodiskcyclicity and codiskcyclicity, introducing and defining codiskcyclicity for collections of linear operators. We establish a criterion for a countable collection of linear operators to be codiskcyclic. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between scodiskcyclicity and codiskcyclicity for collections of operators. Additionally, we demonstrate that the shift operator $S$ is scodiskcyclic on $L^p(\mu)$, under specific conditions where $\mu$ is a positive measure with infinite support.

A common issue in vector magnetic field data analysis is the presence of bias in measurements due to instrumental limitations. This problem is often solved using a minimum energy algorithm, but our research indicates that this approach can introduce artificial correlations between measurements, which we've found to be underreported in the literature. We've developed a straightforward method to quantify this artificial correlation, which we've applied to evaluate the energy bias in a widely used energy algorithm. Our analysis reveals that this algorithm's energy minimization is not sufficient to eliminate the instrumental bias in vector magnetic field measurements. We've also discovered that the artificial correlation generated by this algorithm is not directly proportional to the type of artificial bias introduced. As an alternative solution, we propose a new energy algorithm that fully minimizes the energy while maintaining non-negative measurements, which we've demonstrated to produce significantly lower artificial correlations between the components of the magnetic field data.

A comprehensive analysis of 20 young star clusters across five nearby galaxies has been conducted to examine their physical radii. These clusters, spanning the galaxies of the Milky Way, M33, M31, and the Local Group galaxy Leo A, were selected based on their ages, which range from 10 million to 150 million years. Various methods were employed to measure the half-light radii of the clusters, utilizing visual inspections, deprojection techniques, and fitting models to their UBV color-magnitude diagrams. The results indicate that the clusters' sizes are comparable to those in the Milky Way, with a notable correlation between their sizes and the densities of their host galaxies. Notably, the cluster in Leo A is significantly larger than expected given its galaxy's low stellar density. Furthermore, the study reveals that the clusters' sizes are influenced by their ages, with older clusters tending to be larger. The research also highlights the role of external forces, such as tidal interactions and the galaxy's gravitational field, in shaping the clusters' sizes. These findings contribute to our understanding of the processes that govern the evolution of young star clusters and have implications for future studies of these celestial objects.

We present a novel approach to calculating the decay of $\eta_c \rightarrow 2\gamma$ using lattice QCD, overcoming the limitation of relying on $e^+e^-$-produced charmonium states for data collection. By applying a photon insertion operator to $\eta_c$ states produced via hadronic processes in $e^+e^-$ collisions or hadronic interactions, we can directly measure the decay width, circumventing the need to use reconstructed $\eta_c \rightarrow e^+e^-$ final states. This approach also enables the determination of the electromagnetic form factor for $J/\psi$ in $e^+e^-$ collisions at low momentum transfer. Our lattice results for the $\eta_c \rightarrow 2\gamma$ decay width and the $J/\psi$ form factor are in good agreement with experimental data and previous theoretical predictions.

The Hubbard sign dilemma is a well-known issue in quantum Monte Carlo simulations that severely limits their effectiveness in modeling certain materials.  This problem arises due to negative probabilities in such simulations.  To overcome this barrier, researchers have developed auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo methods that restructure the Hamiltonian, albeit with considerable computational costs.  A breakthrough study has demonstrated the potential of employing complex-valued neural networks to address the Hubbard sign dilemma directly, without restructuring the Hamiltonian.  By training these networks to generate auxiliary-field configurations with positive weights, the model achieves a significant reduction in variance during fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo simulations.  Notably, this neural network approach yields more accurate results than conventional auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo methods for a variety of two-dimensional and three-dimensional models, including the single-band Hubbard model and the spinless Fermi-Hubbard dimer.

We're examining the proportion of $n$-tuples of integers within the range $[1,x]$ that have no common divisor greater than 1 and whose sum equals a given integer $k$. As the number of tuples increases, we find that this proportion behaves similarly to the Dickman function $\rho(k-1)$ when $k$ is much smaller compared to the maximum possible sum $Sn$. We also explore how this behavior changes when $k$ is much larger than $Sn$, and we're able to refine an earlier conjecture by making it more precise.

This work extends the concepts of topological entropy and factor complexity to infinite words, strings over free groups, and topological dynamical systems derived from monoid homomorphisms. We investigate how these measures respond to changes in free group bases and monoid homomorphisms, revealing that entropy and complexity behave in analogous ways under certain conditions. Specifically, we establish a formula for topological entropy based on free group basis alterations, and demonstrate that non-synchronizable uniform morphisms preserve topological entropy. Furthermore, this research provides a topological interpretation for recent findings on the growth rate of subword factors in infinite words.

The current trend of building large-scale AI models that cover multiple tasks is being hindered by the lack of suitable datasets. These datasets need to be both diverse in terms of content and structured in a way that facilitates various types of machine learning applications. To address this issue, we introduce a new dataset called MultiPar, which consists of eight distinct classification and clustering tasks derived from an existing large-scale image dataset. Our analysis of this dataset reveals interesting patterns of content similarity that can be used to improve clustering performance without the need for labeled data. By using this potential for mutual benefit between tasks, we demonstrate significant improvements in clustering accuracy when using retrieval-augmented methods. These results suggest that there exists a form of generalization across different tasks that can be exploited to create more effective data-driven models.

This paper presents a new hyper-accurate and robust variant of the K-RICA
algorithm, an advanced technique for blind source separation (BSS) that
incorporates super-resolved frequency estimation. We adapt the Kullback-
Leibler maximization initialization method to our improved algorithm,
maintaining its computational efficiency. Our simulation results indicate that
the a-M-ar-K-RICA algorithm outperforms the original K-RICA algorithm in
scenarios with high noise levels.

This paper offers an overview of requirements engineering methods tailored for the gaming sector. 
The rise of the gaming sector has resulted in heightened competition, necessitating innovative approaches to meet consumer demands. 
Various requirements techniques applicable to the gaming industry are examined, along with existing research studies and available tool support. 
The document also highlights the key differences between traditional and gaming-focused approaches, along with the main challenges and opportunities for further development within this field.

As a powerful tool for pattern recognition, deep learning has been widely applied in various domains, including image classification and speech recognition. However, these models often rely on vast amounts of private data, raising significant concerns about data privacy. This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of different hyperparameter optimization methods within the framework of differentially private deep learning. We specifically focus on the impact of optimizing key hyperparameters, such as learning rate, on the performance of a trained neural network under privacy constraints. Our experiments, conducted using the MNIST dataset, demonstrate that hyperparameter tuning can enhance the accuracy of a trained network by up to 10%, even when using a minimal budget for differential privacy. Furthermore, we propose a novel method for optimizing hyperparameters by employing a population-based training approach combined with a modified DP-SGD learning rate rule. This method yields a 5% improvement in accuracy over the baseline, without incurring any additional privacy budget. We believe our findings provide valuable insights for researchers working on private deep learning, and the proposed method can be readily integrated into existing frameworks to achieve privacy-preserving performance improvements.

A specific type of algebraic structure, known as an algebra, is examined, consisting of mappings on a set that remain unchanged when reversed. The focus of this paper is on a particular class of algebras, called involutive algebras. Researchers are particularly interested in finding the "Boolean structures" within this category, by redefining the algebra's operation to create a distributive lattice. The paper aims to characterize these structures, by identifying the necessary conditions for an involutive algebra to be transformed into a specific type of structure, known as an RS-algebra, by modifying its operation. The paper also explores the relationship between these structures and another type of algebra, called Post algebras, and provides a class of n-ary operations that can be used to distinguish these Boolean structures.

The Euclid optical imaging system (VIS) will be a key component of the Euclid mission, which is set to significantly enhance our understanding of the universe's structure and evolution. The VIS device is designed to have excellent sensitivity and high quantum efficiency, with 10 scientific cameras working in unison to provide a wide and efficient field of view. However, the close proximity of the detectors means that they may experience correlated noise due to shared readout electronics, which could impact the accuracy of measurements. A detailed analysis of this effect has been conducted, and the results show that correlated noise could introduce a bias in flux measurements, which in turn could affect the reliability of photometric redshift estimates. To mitigate this issue, a new method for flux measurement has been proposed, which is expected to reduce the bias to an acceptable level. The proposed method is expected to be applicable to the Euclid mission and could also be relevant to other imaging missions in the future.

To investigate how stellar populations form in the Milky Way disk, we used a statistical approach to analyze the composition of 102 APOGEE-2 stars. By comparing the chemical differences between these stars to a theoretical model of two-component coagulation, we were able to identify two distinct groups of stars with similar properties. These groups were found to correlate with the ages of the stars, with younger stars having more diverse chemical compositions. We also discovered that the difference in chemical compositions between these groups was influenced by the rotation of the galaxy. This study provides valuable insights into the formation of stellar communities in the Milky Way disk and highlights the importance of using chemical data to map these communities.

The rapid spread of misinformation on social media during the COVID-19 pandemic poses a significant threat to public information security. To understand the underlying factors driving the dissemination of online rumors, we developed a model incorporating government information release, the transmission of official information and misinformation among the public, as well as the influence of external information on public behavior. Through numerical simulations, we analyzed the conditions under which misinformation becomes widespread. Furthermore, we assessed the impact of key parameters on the propagation of misinformation. Our study revealed that a higher rate of government information release and a higher proportion of rational individuals can limit the spread of online rumors. Additionally, a higher level of external information can reduce the dissemination of misinformation. These findings provide valuable insights for preventing the spread of online rumors during public health crises.

We are starting the Fornax3D initiative to create a comprehensive 3D map of the Fornax galaxy cluster, which is a key example of an intermediate-age cluster. Our goal is to study the evolution of galaxies in this cluster by mapping its components in 3D space. To do this, we are using a novel approach that combines cutting-edge data analysis techniques with a distributed computing system. Our project focuses on obtaining precise distances to galaxies in the cluster by analyzing their planetary nebulae, which are reliable cosmic distance indicators. By using a machine learning algorithm, we are able to automatically identify these nebulae in the Hubble Space Telescope images of the cluster galaxies. Our team has already processed a significant amount of data from 11 galaxies in the cluster, and our results show that our algorithm is highly effective at detecting these nebulae. Our project is being carried out on a distributed computing system, which allows us to process a large amount of data efficiently. In the coming years, our team plans to process even more data from the cluster galaxies, which will provide a more complete 3D map of the Fornax galaxy cluster.

Every moment, a vast amount of data is generated by various sources like sensors, social media platforms, and mobile devices. To efficiently process this massive amount of information, stream computing frameworks have been developed. However, existing systems are optimized for handling large-scale data processing tasks, resulting in significant overhead. Consequently, they are not suitable for processing data with relatively low volumes. Our new stream processing engine, called LifeStream, is designed to handle data that is generated periodically and efficiently process it with minimal system overhead. LifeStream achieves this by leveraging a novel architecture that utilizes a single-threaded event loop to handle data processing tasks, thus eliminating the need for heavy system resources. Our evaluations demonstrate that LifeStream outperforms existing stream computing frameworks by up to 4 orders of magnitude in terms of latency, while also being capable of being extended to handle more complex data processing tasks.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in tl(R^4), can be considered as Bertrand curves when placed in relation to their own gyatodes curves. A subset of these curves, defined by a parameter 'a', can be classified as curves of type (1,2). The paper also identifies the functions that describe these curves of type (1,2) in the tl(R^4) space. Furthermore, a distinct category of curves is identified, where curves of type (2,3) exist for a particular value of the parameter 'a', specifically when 'a' equals 3/5.

This paper presents the findings of a study examining the impact of loss function changes in a deep learning-based classifying system. The research aims to provide insights into the effect of loss function alterations on the model's performance and potential improvements in the model's design. The study is conducted to equip non-expert practitioners with a deeper understanding of the loss function's role in the overall system's performance and to facilitate better decision-making when adapting the model to specific application requirements. The results of the study are presented using a classifying system for German traffic signs as an example, with the experimentally obtained results being made available for replication and further analysis.

This article investigates a boundary feedback control system for the Navier-Stokes equations in a bounded two-dimensional domain with a smooth edge. The feedback control is applied at an internal boundary component that is angled relative to the fluid flow, and it has been demonstrated that a linear feedback control mechanism can ensure the system's stability in a probabilistic sense. Additionally, it has been shown that nonlinear feedback controls can achieve asymptotic stability. These results contribute to the broader understanding of flow stabilization through boundary controls, particularly in the context of angle-controlled controls.

This research utilizes a highly detailed thermomechanical model to simulate microstructure formation in amorphous polystyrene. The model incorporates the Becker-Domingos viscoelastic model and employs a finite element method for mechanical analysis. Experimental data from differential scanning calorimetry, stress relaxation tests, and mechanical stretching were employed to validate the model. The simulation reveals the material's glass transition behavior, including stress buildup and heat release, as well as strain-induced crystallization. The model successfully captures the material's response to various loading conditions, yielding results that closely match experimental observations.

To investigate the impact of spin-flip interactions on the triplet nematic state, we calculated the magnetic susceptibility within the Ginzburg-Landau framework. Our calculations indicate that triplet pairs contribute to the spin component of the nematic order parameter through a finite gap, whereas the non-Abelian component remains unbroken until a transition of second order occurs. As a result, the triplet pairs exhibit finite Pauli susceptibility within the nematic phase, which can be harnessed to experimentally distinguish between the two phases. Furthermore, we derived the phase diagram for a model featuring s-wave impurity scattering and weak spin-flip interactions, showing that the first-order transition between the two phases can be influenced by the nematic interaction and the g-factor.

A significant obstacle in creating effective robotic assistants is the difficulty in conveying the right actions to convey the right actions to a robot by its human operator. This challenge is particularly prevalent in scenarios that require a robot to navigate through complex, ever-changing environments. This paper presents a new, adaptable meta-algorithm that leverages feedback from a human operator who provides guidance on the actions taken by the robot. This meta-algorithm is designed to be easily adaptable to various learning methods and can be fine-tuned to meet the specific needs of a given human operator. Through a series of computer simulations and real-world experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in improving the robot's ability to learn from corrective feedback.

A novel differential detection technique for continuous phase modulation (CPM) is examined, specifically focusing on minimizing delay in the differential detection process.  The paper analyzes the performance of this method under various L1 differential detection delay settings and presents the optimal choice of delay.  The proposed approach is demonstrated to be more efficient than existing differential detection schemes by improving the optimal delay minimum Euclidean distance.  The effectiveness of this technique is also verified through simulation results.

Current remote sensing techniques for identifying rain are limited by their reliance on visible light images, which often appear normal even during rainy conditions. To overcome this limitation, using infrared images could provide a more reliable detection method, as raindrops are visible in such images. However, this approach necessitates the creation of realistic infrared images from visible ones, a task that current cross-domain translation methods struggle to accomplish due to the significant disparity between the two domains. In this study, we introduce a novel approach that simultaneously generates and removes rain by leveraging disentangled visible image translation. Our method employs two disentangled visible image translation networks, each responsible for a distinct task, and incorporates a shared latent space to facilitate the sharing of rain-related information. To further enhance the realism of the created rain, we introduce a texture loss function that encourages the preservation of local spatial patterns. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, which outperforms existing approaches in terms of both visual and quantitative metrics.

A prominent approach to solving the reward learning problem is Multi-Armed Bandit with Clustered Rewards (MAB-CCR). In this scenario, the underlying reward structure is divided into distinct clusters, and the optimal arm belongs to a specific cluster that the algorithm must identify. The primary goal of the algorithm is to maximize cumulative regret over time. In this paper, we introduce a novel Visually Aided Cluster Ranking (VACR) algorithm that outperforms the current state-of-the-art method by achieving an optimal large-time asymptotic regret bound. Theoretically, the VACR algorithm's regret bound is O(log T) and can be optimized by adjusting the number of sample arms and sampling time. A key advantage of the VACR algorithm is its ability to reduce the required rank condition for optimal arm identification, making it more flexible and efficient. The VACR algorithm's performance is demonstrated through numerical experiments that show significant improvements in cumulative regret compared to the current state-of-the-art method.

The ongoing debate over the continuum hypothesis's validity within set theory has reached a stalemate, with the lack of a suitable model for understanding its intricacies being a significant barrier. This paper delves into the potential of employing the concept of finiteness from discrete mathematics, specifically through the lens of the Peano axioms, to shed light on the continuum issue. By adopting this approach, we can reframe the question of cardinality in terms of recursive functions, thus providing a more accessible means of comprehension. This reformulation, in turn, enables us to grasp the limitations imposed by diagonalization and to appreciate the significance of effective constructibility. Ultimately, this perspective offers a deeper understanding of the various proposals put forth to address the continuum issue, with the hope of shedding new light on the matter.

The research proposes a new approach to measuring the risk of medication misuse by using the Five Factor Model of character. This model evaluates personality traits across five dimensions: extraversion, openness, honesty, emotional stability, and conscientiousness. To test this hypothesis, a dataset from 1,000 individuals who completed an online survey was analyzed. The survey included questions to assess personality traits and medication usage history. Using a support vector machine algorithm, the study found that personality traits can effectively predict individuals' likelihood of misusing medication, with a 90% accuracy rate. The research suggests that incorporating personality-based scoring into medication risk assessment could enhance the accuracy of risk prediction.

We introduce a novel approach to problem-solving through a set of rules known as Machine Common Sense (MCS). Building on the concept of MCS, we create a dataset called "Atomic", an Atlas of Machine Common Knowledge, which consists of 12,000 everyday problems and 30,000 corresponding rules across multiple categories. These rules are simple, universal statements describing how common objects function, such as doors opening, lights turning on, and appliances operating. We then explore the potential of this data to enhance the reasoning capabilities of machines, using "Atomic" to train models that can solve causal problems, make inferences based on similarity, and solve problems they have never encountered before. Our experiments show that using "Atomic" significantly improves model performance on these tasks, with the most notable improvement being a 15% increase in accurately predicting the effects of actions, compared to models without access to this type of general knowledge.

This paper presents NISQ-PCA, a new portfolio optimization method that uses PCA to reduce the complexity of a HHL system solution. By integrating the solution of the linear equations solved by quantum computers with the dimensionality reduction capabilities of classical principal component analysis, NISQ-PCA offers a practical solution for financial applications on near-term quantum computers. The hybrid approach leverages the strengths of both classical and quantum computing technologies to improve the efficiency of portfolio optimization, ultimately leading to better investment strategies.

Recently, pre-trained language models have significantly advanced natural language processing tasks. To bridge the modality gap, researchers have explored cross-modal training techniques. In this study, we introduce a novel bidirectional training approach that incorporates both unimodal and multimodal learning. Our method utilizes a speech-text dataset to fine-tune pre-trained speech recognition models and language models. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed training approach yields substantial improvements over baseline methods on both speech recognition and language understanding tasks. Notably, our results indicate that models trained with both modalities outperform those trained with only one modality. Furthermore, our method achieves a 9.5% reduction in training time and a 10.5% decrease in training memory usage. To make our approach more accessible, we have made our code and data publicly available at https://github.com/SeunghyunLee/SBFT-SR.

The problem of finding the average width of convex shapes is longstanding in geometric probability. We introduce the concept of average cross section shapes and demonstrate that there is an upper limit to their average width. This limit is achieved by a specific shape known as the Reuleaux triangle. A unique property of average cross section shapes is that their average cross section is always a standard convex shape. We also examine the average area of these shapes, as well as their perimeter, and investigate the average area of complex, self-intersecting curves.

As the size $n$ of a group of uniformly selected numbers from $\{1, \dots, n\}$ increases, the parking process ultimately yields a set of parking functions also drawn from $\{1, \dots, n\}$. By normalizing the initial $n$ numbers to the range $\{1, \dots, 1\}$, a distinct distribution emerges that defines the limiting behavior of any specific number in this sequence. Notably, this distribution is not geometric, and it is shown to be equivalent to the ratio of two independent exponential variables with distinct parameters.

Researchers investigated the electrical properties of superconducting NbN nanowires, which were so narrow that their thermal energy was lower than the superconducting gap. The study found that when the wires were cooled below their critical temperature, their resistance dropped to zero, and the superconducting state's coherence length was larger than both the BCS and dephasing lengths. The application of a magnetic field caused the wires to lose their superconductivity, and the researchers observed that the normal state conductance of the wires was quantized in units of $e^2/h$. The study also found that the conductance of the wires was influenced by a gate voltage, and the data could not be explained by either quantum phase-slip models or the Coulomb blockade model. The researchers proposed that the conductance of the wires was a result of a combination of both models.

The discovery of T-dwarf stars, which are low-mass objects, began with Gliese 229 B in 1995. Initially mistaken for a brown dwarf, it was later identified as an exoplanet due to its unique spectral characteristics. Despite being an exoplanet, GJ 229 B exhibits an unusually high surface temperature of 450-550 K, which is significantly lower than expected. This study utilizes the new APOLLO spectral analysis tool to investigate the spectral characteristics of GJ 229 B and compare its findings with previous research. The results suggest that the high surface temperature of GJ 229 B may be attributed to a combination of factors, including a high albedo, heat generated by tidal forces, and a high atmospheric opacity. This study also reveals that the spectral characteristics of GJ 229 B are inconsistent with a single explanation, which suggests that the high albedo hypothesis may be incorrect. Further research is needed to investigate the spectral characteristics of GJ 229 B in order to better understand its nature.

Current methods for predicting driving scenes rely heavily on a single representation, which has its limitations. To overcome this, we propose a novel approach that utilizes a dual representation, combining semantic and visual features. This approach allows for more accurate and realistic driving scene predictions, even when using relatively low-resolution input images. Our method employs a two-stream network to extract visual features and a knowledge graph to capture semantic information. We then use a generative model to generate high-quality driving scenes that are consistent with the input images. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art driving scene prediction methods on two widely used benchmarks.

Evaluating the inter-orbital interaction is crucial for accurately modeling complex materials with multiple orbitals, yet its direct measurement has been challenging. In this study, we present the first direct experimental determination of the inter-orbital interaction between $d_{xy}$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ electrons in Li$_2$IrO$_3$. Utilizing a comprehensive model and spectroscopic data from angle-resolved photoemission and $K$-edge linearly polarized x-ray absorption spectroscopy, we determined the inter-orbital interaction to be approximately 0.6 eV. This value is notably lower than the on-site Coulomb repulsion of 2.0 eV, a finding that is significant for the development of an appropriate Hamiltonian to describe the magnetic properties of this material.

Einstein's 1911 theory proposed that light could experience diffraction and birefringence due to vacuum fluctuations, a concept later confirmed by the 1999 gravitational birefringence experiment. This experiment, however, was limited by the inability to detect the extremely small birefringence effect. To overcome this limitation, a novel experimental setup is proposed that utilizes a Mach-Zehnder interferometer with a birefringent crystal to detect and distinguish between diffraction and birefringence effects. This experiment could be carried out with current technology, and its results would offer a more direct and precise method for detecting the quantum vacuum's gravitational birefringence effect.

This paper presents a novel method to identify fully transitive polyhedra, building upon the work of G. Orel. Our approach utilizes the group of symmetries to generate a set of transitive 3D shapes, which can then be analyzed to determine if they are fully transitive. This method streamlines the verification process by focusing on the properties of the symmetry group rather than examining all possible configurations. As an illustration, we apply our method to a specific polyhedron, known as the Brouwer 252, and provide a proof of its intransitivity. Furthermore, we list 24 polyhedra that are not intransitive under the action of their respective symmetry groups, and pose an open question regarding the enumeration of such shapes.

We revisit the concepts of unforgeable encryption and authentication introduced by Stern in 1993, specifically examining their one-way security properties. Stern originally proved that no secure unforgeable encryption schemes exist when messages and keys have the same length. In this study, we generalize Stern's results by considering messages and keys of different lengths, and we provide a specific transformation that can convert any unforgeable encryption scheme into an unforgeable authentication scheme, given that the keys are longer than the messages.

Physical layer authentication has gained significant interest in securing communications against unauthorized access. Unlike traditional methods, it doesn't require users to remember passwords or exchange keys, as authentication is based on the unique characteristics of the communication channel. Although researchers have made substantial progress in developing accurate verification methods in controlled environments, their effectiveness in uncontrolled settings remains unclear. Our study focuses on evaluating the authenticity of observed channels in noisy environments, using a simple method to distinguish between similar channels. We collected a large dataset of observed channels and tested various classification methods to determine the most accurate way to authenticate them. Our results indicate that even a basic method can accurately verify the authenticity of observed channels in noisy environments. Moreover, our study shows that the accuracy of verification methods improves with an increase in the number of samples collected. These findings suggest that physical layer authentication may be a reliable method for authenticating users in uncontrolled settings.

We investigated the flat-band surface plasmon polariton (FB-SPP) in twisted transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) and discovered that adding a second TMD layer can enhance the FB-SPP field's concentration. Specifically, we studied a twisted bilayer MoS$_2$ with a 26.56$^{\circ}$ twist angle and found its FB-SPP can be excited by a single photon, leading to a highly localized, intense near-field. This near-field exhibits a "hot spot" with an average enhancement of 10$^4$ compared to conventional FB-SPP in a single TMD. Furthermore, our research indicates that the maximum enhancement of the twisted bilayer MoS$_2$ is 1.5 times greater than that of a single TMD.

The dynamics of the Earth's magnetosphere are heavily influenced by the solar wind, a type of stellar radiation emitted by the Sun. The Sun's surface is constantly covered in solar flares and coronal mass ejections, which are sudden releases of magnetic energy that produce intense bursts of X-rays and radio waves. These events can also eject vast amounts of plasma from the Sun's surface, traveling through space at speeds up to 3,000 km/s. When these bursts of plasma reach the Earth, they interact with the Earth's magnetic field, causing the magnetosphere to shrink and expand. This process can also cause geomagnetic storms, which can disrupt the Earth's atmosphere and affect the behavior of animals that migrate using the Earth's magnetic field. In this review, we discuss the similarities and differences between the Sun's and the Sun's magnetosphere, and how they are affected by the same processes.

Spin-orbit proximity effect is a significant phenomenon in magnetic thin films adjacent to heavy-metal layers, which can significantly affect the overall magnitude of spin-orbit torque in those materials. Spin Hall and spin-orbit torque effects are commonly modeled using a two-current model, which treats the heavy-metal and magnetic layers as separate entities. However, this model overlooks the crucial role of spin-orbit scattering at the interface between the two layers. In this research, a spin-diffusion model is developed to account for spin-orbit scattering in Bi/Co multilayer, and the resulting model is compared to experimental data obtained from measurements of the spin-orbit torque efficiency. The results demonstrate that the new model provides a more accurate representation of the observed data, whereas the conventional two-current model fails to accurately capture the observed data. Furthermore, the research indicates that the spin current generated by the spin Hall effect is significantly affected by the relative thickness of the Bi/Co layers, which has important implications for the design of magnetic memory devices.

This study utilizes the Jumarie type fractional derivative to analyze the fractional Schrödinger equation for a generalized Mie-like potential in multiple dimensions. By applying the semi-classical approximation method, exact solutions for the fractional Schrödinger equation are obtained for this potential. Additionally, a Jumarie type fractional derivative is used to solve the problem via the fractional Adomian decomposition method. The method's effectiveness and accuracy are confirmed through comparative analysis with numerical results.

This method leverages the fact that a significant portion of neural network weights must remain small to maintain this proportionality. We demonstrate that this approach is mathematically equivalent to constraining the network's sensitivity to input variations, thereby ensuring its ability to model the proportional relationship. This method is particularly effective in scenarios where the network is trained on noisy data, as it reduces the network's ability to memorize random fluctuations. This method is shown to be more efficient than traditional regularization techniques, as it directly targets the network's sensitivity to input variations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a series of experiments on various datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and the Street View House Numbers dataset. The results show that this method significantly improves the network's ability to generalize to new data, while maintaining a high level of accuracy. The results also indicate that this method is particularly effective in scenarios where the network is trained on a large amount of data, as it significantly reduces the network's ability to overfit. propose a simplified model that replicates the Basque agreement system with
95.5% accuracy. This simple model suggests that the network is using a
simplified version of the Basque grammar to make predictions about the form
of the auxiliary verb.

Astronomers have observed the light curve of HD 80606 b from multiple sites around the globe, which has allowed for a more precise determination of its orbital parameters. This breakthrough has significant implications for the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope, which will be used to study the planet's thermal radiation in greater detail. By employing a technique known as Sympie, researchers were able to achieve a level of precision that is below the threshold of uncertainty for the time of the planet's maximum brightness. This level of precision is crucial for the effective use of the James Webb Space Telescope, which will be used to study the planet's thermal radiation in greater detail.

The popularity of video games has led to significant advancements in gaming technology, which can be leveraged to enhance human motor control through a novel biofeedback system. This system, which incorporates a motion sensor and a 3D model, utilizes input from the patient to provide real-time feedback and adjust the game's difficulty to optimize learning. Research on adaptive biofeedback systems has shown promising results in improving motor control, but further research is needed to develop customized adaptive algorithms for rehabilitating patients with motor control impairments. This study aims to explore the potential of utilizing models of baseline play in an adaptive biofeedback system, with the ultimate goal of creating a tailored system for physical rehabilitation.

This paper offers a novel perspective on functionals previously studied by Braides, De Giorgi, and Franzoni, specifically those defined on maps that are either broken or rigid. We propose a novel approximation method for these functions, which has significant implications for obtaining novel proofs of existing results and proving new theorems related to phase-field regularization of the given functions. We also explore connections with ball-stiffening models.

This study examines the Drell-Yan process for producing a charged lepton pair, with one lepton being detected, in the context of a specific type of standard extension, the three-generation gauge vector leptoquark model. Calculations for this process at next-to-leading order in QCD, including simulations for parton showers, are presented for the leptoquark and anti-quark colliding scenarios. Additionally, the potential for distinguishing between different types of leptoquarks is explored through kinematic variable analysis and simulated experimental data.

Recent advancements in PET technology have significantly reduced the required radiation dose for imaging, but current low-dose PET scanners still produce images with poor quality. These images often fail to meet the needs of medical professionals due to excessive noise levels. While noise-reduction techniques have been developed, most of them struggle with low-dose PET images that contain complex patterns and are outside the training data distribution. This limitation results in the generation of inaccurate images with unrealistic details. This research focuses on creating a new reduced-dose PET imaging method that utilizes a neural network guided by physical principles and manages data distribution shifts effectively. The proposed model leverages a dual-input neural network to process low-dose PET images and a corresponding low-dose PET scan of the same organ, using Bayesian probability theory to manage data distribution shifts and reduce the impact on the noise levels in the images. This approach allows the model to reduce the noise levels in low-dose PET images by adjusting the variance of the images' Gaussian distribution. The results from the proposed model show a significant improvement in image quality metrics such as PSNR and SSIM, outperforming existing reduced-dose PET imaging methods.

We then examine how designing customized content can be achieved while safeguarding users' personal data. We introduce two cryptographic protocols, one based on public information and another on encrypted data, which allow for the creation of customized content without exposing users' private information. We also explore the limitations of these approaches in the context of Shannon's communication theory. We demonstrate the efficacy of our encrypted-data protocol through a case study involving the customization of music playlists. We also consider the role of public information in assessing its impact on the amount of personalized leakage.
