This paper investigates the relevance of centering theory within the context of neural coreference resolution models. By integrating linguistic background knowledge into a pre-trained BERT model, we assess its impact on coreference recognition performance. A comprehensive dataset of 1000 manually annotated examples is used to evaluate various centering theory metrics, including the most prominent list and the best-matching theory. The results indicate that augmenting the model with centering theory features enhances the baseline model's performance, with a notable improvement of 4 F1 points achieved with the best-matching theory feature. To facilitate future research, the accompanying code and data are made openly accessible at https://github.com/ahmadsharifi/centering-theory-coreference-resolution.

This paper provides an overview of recent research into the parametric complexity of various graph drawing problems, including upward planarity. Upward planarity is a specific constraint for directed graphs, where edges must be drawn above the bounding box of the vertices and follow the direction of the edges. Recent studies have focused on the parametric complexity of solving upward planarity for specific graph types, such as trees and series-parallel graphs. These investigations have also led to the development of new parameterized algorithms for recognizing and constructing series-parallel graphs.

This paper outlines our approach to automating system setup, a crucial yet frequently overlooked aspect of replicating and contributing to research. We are developing an automated system configuration tool that allows researchers to easily set up and run their projects on various systems. This tool will streamline the process of installing necessary software, configuring system settings, and running experiments, thereby facilitating smoother collaboration and contribution to open-source initiatives. We are currently developing this tool using Rust and will present our progress at the Repl.it event.

The operator expansion method has long been used to study hadronic processes, yet its connection to the parton-hadron duality remains unclear. This study aims to shed light on this issue by examining the entanglement of the operator expansion within a simple model. The results obtained through this examination are then compared to the duality between partons and hadrons.

Using WiFi signals to estimate distances between devices has gained significant attention in recent years due to their ability to provide accurate measurements for creating indoor maps and enabling location-based services. This paper presents a novel approach to WiFi-based range estimation that leverages machine learning techniques to create a mapping between signal characteristics and distances between devices. We employ a dataset comprising 1000 measurements between two devices in a controlled environment and utilize various machine learning algorithms to develop a method for estimating distances. Our proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods, achieving a mean error of just 0.5 meters. This breakthrough has the potential to enhance the accuracy of location-based services and indoor mapping systems, ultimately providing more reliable and efficient solutions for a wide range of applications.

We employ a semi-analytical method to examine the long-term stability of a Dyson sphere, a structure that orbits a black hole. Our analysis reveals that minor structural imperfections within the Dyson shell can lead to its collapse due to the influence of gravitational waves. To maintain stability, it is necessary to either increase the number of structural components or allow for their relative movement. Furthermore, our model predicts that the components of the Dyson shell will gradually move towards positions of maximum gravitational wave frequency, resulting in an increase in the number of segments over time. This growth rate is determined by the mass of the black hole and the inherent properties of the structural material.

In today's interconnected world, businesses heavily rely on interconnected systems to deliver goods and services to their customers. As a result, ensuring that contractual obligations are met becomes crucial for maintaining trust and reliability. This paper proposes a groundbreaking approach to identifying breaches of agreement in service-oriented environments by utilizing peer-to-peer technology. By integrating this technology with machine learning-based data analysis, we can achieve accurate and timely identification of breaches in a decentralized manner, without the need for a central authority. This approach has the potential to revolutionize the way businesses operate and interact with their customers, paving the way for a more efficient and reliable global marketplace.

A novel method to mitigate beam disruption instability in energy recovery linacs is proposed by optimizing the transverse beam profile. This proposed solution involves introducing controlled beam asymmetry and shifting the beam's position, effectively decreasing beam-peering interactions and enhancing longitudinal beam stability. The method's benefits are demonstrated through a case study on the CLIC energy recovery linac, where the beam disruption instability is shown to be significantly suppressed by implementing the suggested measures. The results indicate that this approach can be universally applied to energy recovery linacs to prevent beam disruption instability.

Scarcity of neutron sources necessitates the development of efficient detection techniques. This research presents a comprehensive analysis of the neutron-proton interaction cross-section, utilizing a 3D scintillator detector with 100% neutron interaction probability. The experiment was conducted with a 10 µA proton beam at 1.85 MeV, and the results were obtained by measuring the neutron emission rate as a function of the detection angle. The measured cross-section data align with theoretical predictions within a 10% margin of error.

This research investigates how the sticking strength of dust particles changes in response to rising temperatures within a protoplanetary disc. The study focuses on the impact of water content and particle size, examining the adhesion forces of particles with diameters of 0.1, 0.5, and 1 micrometers across a temperature range of 10 to 150 Kelvin. The experiments utilize a technique called quasielastic torsional balance to measure the adhesion forces of particles with these characteristics. The findings indicate that particles with lower temperatures and higher water content exhibit stronger sticking strengths, which is a critical factor in the formation of planetary bodies within protoplanetary discs. The study's results are also compared to the conditions present in different regions of a protoplanetary disc, specifically the inner, middle, and outer regions. The research reveals that particles with lower temperatures and higher water content are more likely to stick together and form larger aggregates, which is a critical step in the formation of planetary bodies within protoplanetary discs. The study's results have significant implications for our understanding of the formation of planetary bodies within protoplanetary discs. Supervised dimension reduction techniques have been extensively studied, with a focus on learning efficient mappings that preserve labeling information in a lower-dimensional space. In this study, an R package for evaluating and visualizing the Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis method is introduced. This package leverages the 'lavaan' and 'ggfortify' libraries to facilitate the implementation of LFDA and provide tools for assessing its performance through various graphical representations, including scatter plots, classification error rates, and confusion matrices. A case study using lung cancer gene expression data demonstrates the LFDA methodology and its effectiveness in visualizing and evaluating the results.

Mimicry learning enables a mobile robot to follow and maintain a safe distance from a target object, such as a car, while navigating through an environment. This research extends previous work on mimicry learning by developing a unified framework that integrates two key components: rigid transformations and obstacle evasion. A unified framework is created to generate a target point that accounts for the target object's orientation and position relative to the surrounding environment. This framework is then used in conjunction with a mimicry learning method that employs artificial potential fields to guide the robot through an environment. The resulting system is tested through simulations and real-world experiments, which demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in enabling the robot to follow and maintain a safe distance from the target object while evading obstacles.

We have calculated the one-loop central-emission vertex for two colorless external bosons in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. Initially, we establish a general formula for the one-loop central-emission vertex applicable to any type of external states. Subsequently, we derive the specific form of this vertex for two bosonic external states, and compare it with the square of the tree-level three-point vertex. Furthermore, we establish a direct relationship between the one-loop central-emission vertex and the four-loop beta function of Yang-Mills theory.

A novel type of superfluid has been predicted to emerge from a spin-singlet state in 2D systems with Rashba spin-orbit coupling. In this study, we investigate the ground state of a 2D Rashba Hubbard model, incorporating a finite spin-orbit coupling strength, under conditions of strong atomic attraction. Our analysis employs a Gutzwiller variational approach, and our findings reveal that the ground state exhibits superfluidity in a specific momentum range, and that this state is spin-singlet in nature, persisting even in the absence of a magnetic field that overcomes the Rashba spin-orbit coupling. Furthermore, our results indicate that the ground state's topological properties are influenced by the interplay between interaction and spin-orbit coupling, and that the ground state exhibits non-trivial Chern numbers in certain regimes, leading to the emergence of a quantum anomalous Hall effect.

Using high-resolution muon-spin relaxation measurements, we have detected a sudden shift in the vortex lattice structure of a cuprate superconductor, YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.95}$, as magnetic flux lines transition from a square-square grid configuration. This observed transition occurs at a temperature of 45 K and 14 mT, which is notably lower than the critical temperature of 93 K. Our findings suggest that the square-square grid phase may be intrinsically linked to the superconducting state of the material.

We've developed a new model for molten polymers with stretched, molten polymer 'brushes' of highly extended chains. These brushes consist of an 'exclusion zone' with very high density at the base, decreasing to zero at the outer edge. We've found that the 'exclusion zone's thickness is significantly larger than that of Parry's stretched disks, and we propose a new formula to describe its radius. We also investigate the 'exclusion zone's volume and its average density, and we discuss the morphology of molten polymer 'brushes' with different substrate geometries.

A graph G is considered resolvable by a set S if the position of every vertex in G can be uniquely determined based on the distances to the elements of S. This property is known as the metric dimension of G. However, the requirement for the sets that satisfy this condition to be the same size is often too restrictive. A newer concept, called shortened metric dimension, was introduced to generalize this idea. It allows for the position of every vertex in the graph to be uniquely determined by a pair of sets, where one set satisfies the original metric dimension requirement and the other set is a separate, distinct set. This concept has been explored for various types of graphs, including paths, cycles, and their products, as well as for graphs with a given maximum degree.

Using the 11-year 0.1 to 3 GeV energy range data from the Fermi-LAT gamma-ray telescope, we produced a comprehensive gamma-ray map of the sky. We then developed an improved version by applying a Bayesian point-source subtraction method. This advanced technique allowed us to create a more accurate all-sky chart and a new list of gamma-ray sources that vary in intensity. Our results show that sources that fluctuate by more than 100% make up 20% of the brightest sources and 40% of the sources that fluctuate by more than 50%. Our study also shows that the gamma-ray background is not uniform, with some areas being up to 100% brighter than others. We believe our research can help astronomers better understand gamma-ray sources and their fluctuations, as well as provide a more accurate gamma-ray background chart.

A well-known ranking system for $n$ agents is serial dictatorship, where agents take turns in an arbitrary order and select their preferred remaining item. We introduce a new, random serial dictatorship mechanism that allows any deterministic strategy-proof method to be weakly Pareto improved relative to it. Notably, this new mechanism has applications in large-scale settings, where it can be implemented in constant time.

We developed an automated system to detect binary asteroids in wide-field images, adapting it for use with the Pan-STARRS1 survey. By analyzing 1.4 million images from 2010-2013, we identified 13 potential binary systems. Our detection method relies on identifying pairs of moving objects within a single image that share the same trajectory, accounting for the image's field of view, sky movement, and the object's movement. To validate our findings, we used the system to search for known binary asteroids in images from the Pan-STARRS1 survey, successfully detecting 10 out of 11 cases. We estimate our system has a 10% chance of correctly identifying our 13 candidates as binary asteroids, with further observations needed to confirm the remaining candidates. We estimate our system has the potential to discover around 10 binary asteroids per 100 million images, and we discuss the characteristics of our candidates and the limitations of our detection method.

This paper proposes a novel approach to estimating and inferring on a specific type of model, one that combines linear and non-linear components, used to analyze relationships in networks. Initially, we develop a method to assess partial relationships within a data set, then apply this approach to study the dynamics of peer influence in a data set from high schools in New Jersey. Our results indicate that a specific type of model, known as an additive exponential family regression, best fits this data set, and the influence parameters vary significantly across different schools.

This study introduces novel expressions for the Leibniz rule under the influence of the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and differential operators. Specifically, new formulas have been derived for the combined application of these operators. Additionally, several existing results have been generalized through this framework.

Variation in wireless channel conditions across a geographic area is common, 
with some locations experiencing better wireless connectivity than others. 
This paper seeks to develop and apply adaptive algorithms that can accurately 
map out spatial patterns of signal variation. Specifically, we focus on models 
that account for multipath fading and provide an analysis of the random 
convergence rate of the proposed algorithm. Next, we apply this algorithm to 
create adaptive beamformers that can maximize signal strength in areas with 
highly variable wireless channels. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness 
of this approach through simulations using real-world data from a wireless 
network.

This paper introduces an updated version of the Python-based visualization tools known as the Scientific Extras for Imaging and Spectral Spectral Data (RCSEDv1).  In response to the growing demand for real-time visualization, we have upgraded the software to incorporate the Matplotlib backend, enabling interactive graphical outputs.  Additionally, we have made significant improvements to the spectroscopic visualization features, and made the software more user-friendly through the inclusion of a command-line interface and a graphical user interface.  We have also made the software more versatile by enabling the integration of third-party plugins, and have made it available on a cloud-based platform through Docker.  We believe that these enhancements will make the software more useful for a wider range of users, including those working in fields outside of astronomy.

A common practice in medical image segmentation is to utilize boundary-sensitive loss functions in a self-supervised framework. However, since this approach relies on a single loss function, it may not be optimal for a self-supervised framework. In this paper, we propose an innovative approach that combines multiple loss functions, which is referred to as boundary-sensitive information optimization loss. This method is designed to effectively capture informative information from both low-level and high-level features. We incorporate this method into a self-supervised framework, which is referred to as Information Optimization Network. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves outstanding performance in terms of mean Dice score and mean 95 Hausdorff distance, which are comparable to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our method exhibits robust performance in terms of generalization ability.

The success of modern board games like Dungeons and Dragons relies heavily on the Dungeon Master's (DM) ability to effectively lead the game and engage players. To achieve this, the DM must possess leadership skills and a theory of mind, enabling them to understand and anticipate the thoughts and desires of their players. In this research, we utilize large language models to simulate DMs and examine how they can effectively lead players with varying theory-of-mind abilities. Our experiments reveal that DMs with limited theory-of-mind abilities struggle to lead effectively, whereas those with more advanced theory-of-mind abilities can anticipate player actions and guide them accordingly. To further investigate this phenomenon, we introduce a novel game called Intents and Theory-of-Mind (IaTM), which pits DMs against players in a competitive setting. Our research provides a foundation for future studies on how DMs can be trained to lead effectively and engage players in virtual reality environments.

A Lexical Semantic Change Detector (LSCC) system was created to identify significant alterations in word meanings. This novel approach leverages the capability of large-scale self-supervised language models to pinpoint words that have undergone a notable shift in meaning. By comparing word vector representations from different time periods, it determines which words have experienced a significant change in their semantic orientation. To refine this process, the authors propose a new metric called Lexical Semantic Shift (LOSS), which quantifies the degree of change in a word's meaning. The proposed method is demonstrated to be effective in identifying alterations in word meanings within the Goldman-Shapiro corpus.

We propose a novel set of functions that depend on $k_\perp$ and $z$, which are related to the transverse momentum and the fraction of the parent hadron's longitudinal momentum. These functions are derived from matrix elements of bilinear quark operators, and we establish connections to T-odd functions like Sivers and Boer-Mian distributions. Additionally, we derive operator identities that relate our novel functions to a set of functions known as quark potential correlators, which have been extensively studied in QCD sum rules. These connections provide a means to study novel (quasi)parton distribution functions using lattice QCD simulations.

The intricate folding and knotting of proteins are influenced by their primary sequences and the topological complexity of their native structures. Understanding the mechanisms behind the formation of knots in proteins requires a detailed analysis of their native structures. This study focuses on protein and homopolymer chains in a solvent, examining their folding pathways from an initial unknotted state to a trefoil-knotted state. By investigating the topological properties of these chains' configurations, researchers found that certain pathways are more likely to occur based on the minimum change in knot complexity, as measured by the Calugareanu-White-Crawford relation. This finding holds true for both proteins and synthetic polymers, suggesting that the pathway of least resistance is determined by the change in twist rather than writhe. This insight is applicable to the study of protein folding and the engineering of DNA nanostructures.

By combining Planck and BOSS data, we can derive precise cosmological parameters and potentially constrain early dark energy (EDE). A key factor in this process is the choice of parameters that describe EDE. We focus on two of these parameters: $f_{\rm RD}$, which represents the total energy density of EDE relative to the critical density at the end of the radiation-dominated era, and $V_\phi$, which represents the potential energy of a scalar field responsible for EDE. We analyze the effect of these parameters on the $N_{\rm eff}$ parameter, which is a key component in the Planck-BOSS likelihood. We then use a method called the profile likelihood to study the effect of $f_{\rm RD}$ and $V_\phi$ on the $N_{\rm eff}$ likelihood. We find that the EDE model with two free parameters is consistent with the Planck-BOSS likelihood, whereas the model with one parameter is inconsistent with the likelihood. We also find that the EDE model with two parameters is consistent with the Planck-BOSS likelihood only for a small range of $V_\phi$ values.

Let $X$ be a symplectic manifold and let $\pi: X \rightarrow B$ be a symplectic map onto another manifold $B$. We define the group $\mathcal{M}(X,\pi)$ to be the collection of all symplectic self-maps of $X$ that preserve the map $\pi$, with a mapping degree of one. This group has an associated exact sequence, where the surrounding terms are the integer lattices generated by the blowup points of $X$, and the group of mapping classes of $B$. We investigate the properties of $\mathcal{M}(X,\pi)$ for various instances of $B$ being the symplectic torus $T^4$ or a blowup of a rational symplectic surface.

We've derived a nonperturbative relationship between the mass gap and the rate of symmetry breaking in both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories. This connection can be expressed as an inequality, where the rate of symmetry breaking is bounded by the theory's mass gap. As a consequence, in theories with a finite mass gap, continuous symmetries cannot be spontaneously broken. We've also established a similar connection in Ginzburg-Landau theory.

Current NLP models excel at making and making correcting predictions,
but understanding what influences their decisions is a complex task.
One proposed method to investigate decision-making is through counterfactuals,
which involve making minimal changes to input data to alter a model's prediction.
Automating this process is a challenging task, as it requires pinpointing specific
word sequences that significantly impact the model's decision-making process.
We explore a novel approach to this problem using a pre-trained language model
to identify these influential word sequences, which we call DISCO.
Our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques on multiple benchmarks,
achieving a 10% improvement in the score of a custom benchmark we created.
Additionally, our results show that our approach effectively captures semantic
causality in both synthetic and real-world datasets.

The total coloring of a graph involves assigning colors to both its edges and vertices with the condition that connected elements in the graph must have different colors. A neighborhood sum distinguishing total coloring is a type of total coloring that ensures each vertex's incident elements receive colors in a differentiated manner. This paper explores the minimum colors needed for such a type of neighborhood sum distinguishing total coloring for specific types of circulant graphs, denoted as Cn(s1, s2,..., sk), where 1 ≤ s1 < s2 <... < sk ≤ [n/2]. The needed colors are determined for graphs formed by one to three parameters, Cn(s1, s2), Cn(s1, s2, s3), under certain conditions for n. The paper also aims to establish the chromatic sum for such neighborhood sum distinguishing total coloring for these types of circulant graphs.

The growth of high-quality Heusler films using remote epitaxy on graphene-covered sapphire substrates is being explored to achieve this on a large scale. A theoretical model has been developed to analyze the balance between different growth modes, including van der Waals, remote, and pinhole epitaxy. This model is applied to understand the equilibrium of magnetic Ni2MnSn films grown on graphene-covered Al2O3. A new parameter is introduced to describe the competition between these modes, and it is found that this balance is influenced by the thickness of the Heusler film, the mechanical stress within the film, and the surface energy at the interface between the film and substrate. A general framework is proposed to predict the growth modes of various Heusler compounds, and the results show that certain compounds, such as Ni2MnSn, Co2MnSi, and Fe2VSn, can be grown in a remote epitaxial mode when they reach a certain thickness.

This research focuses on a specific code type known as $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, for prime numbers $p$ greater than two. We establish the connection between the code's rank and the maximum rank achievable, for each prime $p$ greater than two. We also identify conditions under which an $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear code reaches its highest possible rank. Additionally, we examine the code's null space dimension and its relation to the code's rank, for each prime $p$ greater than two. We provide a method to construct an $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear code with a specific rank, for any prime $p$ greater than two. We demonstrate this method's effectiveness by creating three distinct $\mathbb{Z}_3\mathbb{Z}_9$-linear codes. We also prove that an $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear code is equivalent to its projection, for any prime $p$ greater than two.

The dynamics of polymer melts being injected through narrow die openings are being influenced by the formation of a 'plug' region, where the material behaves differently due to its exposure to less intense shear forces. Understanding the properties and structure of this plug is crucial in designing injection molds and predicting final product quality. In this study, we used rheological models and direct numerical simulations to examine the properties of the plug region, specifically its structure, material flow, and internal stress patterns. Our findings show that the plug region is characterized by a distinct flow profile, with a 'core' region exhibiting little to no stress and a 'skin' region experiencing significant stress and heat. The thickness of this skin region is determined by the die opening size and the polymer's molecular weight. The study also found that the plug region's internal stress patterns are influenced by the die's shape and the injection speed. These findings have important implications for predicting final product quality and optimizing polymer processing techniques.

Single-label data annotation techniques are widely used in various fields due to their efficiency in quickly classifying entire samples. In contrast, multi-label annotation techniques require precise control over each sample's individual labels, making them more time-consuming and costly. This paper presents a novel method for automatically generating multi-label datasets from single-label data, by using active learning to select and annotate samples that are missing certain labels. The results show that the proposed method can efficiently create high-quality multi-label datasets from single-label data, with the added benefit of being able to use the same data for both types of annotation. The results also indicate that the proposed method outperforms existing baselines in terms of classification accuracy.

This research provides a diminishing energy upper bound for the time fractional Allen-Cahn equation and its variant with the Hele-Shaw force. The study also introduces the spatial fractional phase-field model and establishes the corresponding energy dissipation inequality for this type of equation.

A well-known correspondence between classical mechanics and quantum mechanics can be mathematically expressed as a functor mapping quantum systems to classical systems. This correspondence is a specific instance of a broader relationship between quantum and classical systems that can be described using category theory. A particular 2-categorical structure, the double lax cosmos, was developed to capture this broader connection. Within this structure, a specific type of cosmos, consisting of symmetric monoidal categories, is mapped to a substructure made of double monoidal categories. A specific instance of this 2-categorical construction is the mapping between the categories of quantum and classical systems.

We propose a novel mechanism to explain gamma-ray emissions from nearby galaxies, utilizing a magnetically captured disk (MCD) model. This model posits that strong magnetic fields in galaxy jets capture the outer regions of accretion disks, resulting in significant gamma-ray production through pion decays. The MCD model is particularly effective in accounting for the gamma-ray emissions from four galaxies - M87, NGC 4258, NGC 1068, and NGC 5548 - which have been observed by the Fermi-LAT. The model successfully matches the energy spectra of these galaxies, as well as the upper limits on the gamma-ray emissions from NGC 3115 and NGC 4889. Furthermore, the MCD model can also account for the gamma-ray emissions from the central supermassive black hole in M87, as detected by the Chandra X-ray Observatory. The model's predictions for the gamma-ray emissions from M87 are consistent with the observed data, and the MCD model is a viable alternative to the traditional disk-jet emission model.

This study examines the optimal portfolio allocation strategy to maximize long-term average logarithmic growth, considering a scenario where investment opportunities are optimal and interconnected. Theoretical models are developed for two primary scenarios: when the number of available investments is fixed and when the number of available investments expands over time. The resulting strategies have practical applications in the design of robust investment frameworks. The concept of an expanding market was initially introduced by Merton in 1992 and further investigated by others in the field. The work presented here offers an alternative approach to the solution of the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-isabel equations, utilizing a specific transformation of the value function. The primary contribution of this study is the extension of the solution to scenarios involving market illiquidity. The results have implications for the implementation of portfolio optimization techniques and the design of portfolio management systems. The research also provides a framework for the development of portfolio management software and investment technology. Early detection of heart disorders relies heavily on accurate sound analysis, which can be achieved through advanced techniques like artificial intelligence. However, these methods struggle with noisy data, commonly encountered in real-world scenarios. To address this challenge, this study proposes a novel deep learning model that combines two innovative approaches: a specialized activation function to handle noisy data and a specific convolutional layer to handle varying data sizes. The proposed model was tested on two widely used datasets, revealing its superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art models. The results indicate significant improvements in accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score, with the proposed model outperforming the best existing model by 10% in accuracy and 11.5% in F1 score. The proposed model's performance was also verified through visualizations and statistical tests, confirming its robustness and generalizability. The proposed model's source code is available on GitHub for further exploration.

The rise of mobile and wearable technologies has enabled individuals to monitor their health and manage chronic conditions more effectively. However, collecting and sharing personal health data poses significant privacy concerns. A federated learning approach has been proposed to address these issues by allowing a central server to train a machine learning model using data from multiple participants without sharing the data itself. Despite this, the limited availability of relevant data at the server and the participating devices hampers the effectiveness of the basic federated learning system. To overcome this challenge, a transfer learning framework has been developed, allowing the server to transfer knowledge from the participants' local data to a target application, with the help of a small amount of target data. A simulation study has been conducted to evaluate the performance of the federated and transfer learning systems, with the results showing that the transfer learning framework outperforms the basic federated learning system in terms of accuracy. A wearable medical care application has been developed to demonstrate the practical use of the transfer learning framework, with the system allowing users to monitor their heart rate variability and receive personalized feedback through a chatbot. A pilot study has been conducted to gather user feedback on the wearable medical care application, with the results indicating high levels of usability, ease of use, and user engagement.

This paper provides a detailed examination of various portfolio optimization methods, specifically those focused on higher-order moments, including Skewness and Kurtosis. It also offers cutting-edge approaches to solving the resulting large-scale quadratic and non-linear optimization problems.

We propose a new approach to the coincidence dilemma, based on a new understanding of the coincidence problem's underlying issue. This approach is not limited to a specific theory of dark matter, but rather addresses the issue of dark matter density fluctuations. To address this issue, we suggest two possible solutions: altering the initial fluctuations or changing the mechanism that forms dark matter. This approach allows us to examine the coincidence dilemma from the perspective of the dark matter formation process, leading to the conclusion that any dark matter model that does not result in the observed scale of superclusters must be considered a "flexible" solution to the coincidence dilemma.

This study presents an innovative approach to automating software quality assessment, which can be utilized for both academic and professional purposes. We have developed a system capable of automatically gathering data from various online sources, conducting quality checks, and disseminating the results through multiple channels, including visual graphs, printed reports, and electronic mail. As a demonstration of our approach, we have created a quality assessment tool specifically designed for online journals, which analyzes critical aspects such as grammar, formatting, and visual presentation. We have also explored the potential for applying this system to other contexts, such as online magazines and newspapers.

This paper addresses a specific control problem in economics where an agent's spending changes abruptly in response to a given signal. We provide a solution to this problem by considering all possible signals that result in spending patterns that are right-continuous with left limits. A key insight is that the optimal signal can be determined by gradually adjusting the current state from its initial value until the present value of future spending equals that of future hypothetical spending. This equality can be established using the theory of monotone operators. We also discuss the implications of this approach in the context of existing research. A specific example is used to illustrate the practical application of these concepts.

Within the context of type-II seesaw leptoquark models, we examine the implications of color-triplet scalar leptoquarks in type-II seesaw models. These leptoquarks, being even under parity, are constrained by experimental data from proton decay and lepton flavor changing processes. A significant advantage of this model is that it allows for the generation of three generations of neutrino masses through the decay of a heavy Higgs boson. A key finding is that lepton flavor violating processes are heavily suppressed, with branching ratios for $ \tau \to \mu \gamma $ and $ \tau \to 3 \mu $ being below current experimental limits. A crucial observation is that the leptoquark masses are within the reach of the Large Hadron Collider, with unequal production rates of two types of leptoquarks, denoted as $ \Delta^+ $ and $ \Delta^{++} $, with $ \Delta^+ $ being produced more frequently. A key signature of this model is the presence of same-sign dileptons, with the $ \Delta^{++} $ being produced in association with a $ \tau^+ $ and a $ \Delta^+ $ being produced in association with a $ \tau^+ $ and a $ \tau^0 $. Deep learning techniques have been effectively utilized in various domains, including medical imaging, electrocardiogram analysis, and other biomedical applications. However, these methods demand substantial amounts of labeled training data, which can be scarce in some domains such as temporal sequence assessment. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach called Guided Learning (GLEARN), which employs a simplified, low-dimensional network to learn temporal sequences with minimal training data. This network is then leveraged to guide a more sophisticated, high-dimensional network through an efficient, end-to-end learning process. In contrast to conventional deep learning methods, GLEARN achieves superior performance with significantly less training data. We validate this approach on two real-world datasets from the life sciences domain, specifically the T cell activation and the fruit fly circadian rhythm cases. Experimental results show that GLEARN outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios with limited training data. Furthermore, GLEARN exhibits the capacity to learn complex dynamics and patterns from real-world data, which can be visualized and analyzed.

To overcome this, galaxies may undergo a process of collapse, which can be initiated by the formation of a sufficiently massive cluster of stars. However, before this occurs, the cooling of a galaxy's gas can be influenced by the emission of a specific type of radiation, known as the C{\sc i} 60 $\mu$m radiation, from a galaxy's molecular gas reservoirs. We propose a vectorlike composite new physics model that can address the observed deviations in the $Flavor$ $Physics$ anomalies within the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) framework. The new physics scale in this model is estimated to be around 10 TeV. The vectorlike particles' contribution to the $Flavor$ $Physics$ anomalies and the Higgs signal strength in the SMEFT framework are calculated at one-loop and tree levels, respectively. The model's predictions are in line with the experimental data, and it offers the possibility of elucidating the $Flavor$ $Physics$ and $B_s \to s\gamma$ anomalies simultaneously. The model's predictions for the SMEFT Wilson coefficients and the fraction of $VV$ Higgs signal strength are estimated to be $10^{-4}$ GeV$^{-2}$ and 0.1, respectively. The model's predictions for the direct new physics searches at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) are also investigated. The model's predictions for the heavy partner of the photon and the $8$ TeV and $13$ TeV LHC searches are estimated to be 4.5 TeV and 5.5 TeV, respectively. The model's predictions for the future 100 fb$^{-1}$ and 3000 fb$^{-1}$ LHC runs are estimated to be 6.5 TeV and 7.5 TeV

Given a positive integer d, we consider the set of all arrangements of n binary strings of length d. If two neighbors in an arrangement differ by at most 2 units, we say the arrangement has a distance of at most 2 units. If every arrangement of m binary strings of length d can be scaled to an arrangement of binary strings with a distance of exactly 2 units, the set of such arrangements is denoted as R_d^*(m). It is proven that R_d^*(m) contains at most the set of arrangements with a distance of exactly 2 units. Furthermore, for every positive integer m, R_d^*(m) is equal to the set of such arrangements with a distance of exactly 2 units if and only if m is less than or equal to the maximum number of arrangements with a distance of exactly 2 units of length d with a specific property. It is also shown that R_d^*(m) contains at most the set of arrangements with a distance of exactly 2 units of length d with a specific property. It is also shown that for every arrangement with a distance of exactly 2 units of length d with a specific property, R_d^*(m) is equal to the set of such arrangements with a distance of exactly 2 units of length d with a specific property if and only if m is less than or equal to the maximum number of such arrangements with a distance of exactly 2 units of length d with a specific property.

This paper introduces a novel approach to enhance musical instrument recognition accuracy by integrating a hierarchical network within a convolutional neural network (CNN) framework. A primary CNN network is initially trained on a large dataset of general instruments, and a secondary, specialized hierarchical CNN network is then developed by incorporating a primary CNN module and a unique sub-network. This new hierarchical network is capable of identifying specific instruments within a larger category, and has been tested in a few-shot learning scenario where only a limited number of samples are available for training. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach yields significant accuracy improvements compared to existing methods in the Musical Instrument Discrimination Dataset (MID) and the RAVDESS datasets.

Researchers have recently proposed using pulsar timing arrays to detect gravitational waves from sources like inspiralling binaries outside the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA network's sensitivity range. To better understand the data that these arrays will provide, the characteristics of such sources must be thoroughly investigated. The current study examines the impact of different parameter estimation methods on the fit of binary systems, specifically focusing on how the choice of waveform model and the order of post-Newtonian terms in the semi-major axis and eccentricity expansions affect the results. The research also explores the computational costs associated with these different models and terms. The findings indicate that while including higher-order terms can improve the results, it comes at the cost of increased computation time. To mitigate this issue, a method is proposed that allows for the use of a computationally efficient approximation of certain terms. The results show that this approximation yields nearly identical outcomes to the exact terms, with a minimal increase in computation time. The proposed method is then employed in a full six-dimensional exploration of a binary system's parameter space, with the findings indicating that certain parameter choices yield the most accurate results with the least computational cost. These results are expected to inform the design of pulsar timing array data analysis pipelines.

We examine the ASEP speed dynamics in a system of size $n$ and observe how the velocity process converges as $n$ increases. This convergence occurs at the rate of $n^{-1/3}$ on a scale of $n^{1/3}$, and the limiting distribution is found to be the Kosterlitz-Thouless-Mandelbom-Walker distribution. This research complements the work of Corwin, Hammond, and Seppalainen (2017) and provides insights into the first and second class particle speeds described by ASEP.

As the ongoing SARS-CoV-2 pandemic continues to spread globally, mathematical models are being employed to study its dynamics and inform public health policy decisions. Various types of these models have been developed and can be categorized based on their underlying assumptions and applications. A systematic overview of these models has been undertaken, covering both simple and complex approaches, as well as their implications for understanding and managing infectious diseases. Additionally, a supplementary section explores the significance of incorporating long-term environmental changes into model design.

We examine the unique quantum state of Majorana fermions, specifically those that follow linear dispersion, and investigate their behavior through statistical methods. By analyzing single-particle data, we develop a way to identify fermionic characteristics and determine the optimal distribution for a non-Majorana fermion. Further, we compare this optimal distribution to the actual Majorana distribution, using a metric called Earth Mover's Distance (EMD). Our analysis reveals that linear Majorana particles exhibit distinct behavior in both the electron density and spin distribution, which can be clearly distinguished from other types of particles. However, when considering multiple particles in a system, the difference between a optimal particle system and a Majorana system becomes less apparent.

Acronyms are frequently encountered in the written word, yet they can be hard to comprehend, particularly when their referents are ambiguous. This issue is prevalent in the web, where numerous documents contain acronym-laden sections that are difficult to navigate. Although existing tools exist to tackle this problem, they are often limited to specific domains, require human intervention, or are confined to particular file formats. To bridge this gap, we present MadDog, a cutting-edge system that acquires, processes, and clarifies acronyms from web sources using automated methods. MadDog employs advanced techniques to extract acronyms from both plain text and formatted documents, while its innovative disambiguation approach leverages state-of-the-art NLP tools to generate descriptive labels for each acronym and its corresponding full form. As an open-source web application, MadDog is freely accessible to anyone and can be utilized to explore the fascinating world of acronyms.

Converting a spinor atom species into a bosonic molecule with spin properties through bond formation is a process worth investigating. This study focuses on analyzing the internal spin states of these fictitious molecules, formed from two spinor atoms, and explores whether they can exhibit spinor-like behavior. By applying closed-loop two-photon transitions, we propose using the molecules' spin states for coherent control and entanglement generation. Furthermore, we examine how weak interactions between these molecules affect their spin dynamics. It is found that for certain conditions, the molecules can maintain their spin coherence for a duration comparable to that of the parent atoms. This capability enables the feasible implementation of spin-based quantum information processing using these molecules.

Due to its high storage density, DNA storage is an attractive option for archiving vast amounts of data. However, certain challenges, including high expenses, slow synthesis speeds, and the need for hierarchical storage, impede its widespread adoption. To address these issues, we propose a new encoding method that enables efficient hierarchy and data refreshes in DNA storage. This method utilizes error-correcting codes, which allow for cost-effective data storage, easy data updates, and fast data refreshes. Our proposed method leverages the inherent error-correcting capabilities of PCR to recover data from lower levels of the storage hierarchy without the need for complex decoding processes. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in storage costs and data refresh speeds when using our proposed method compared to traditional storage and refresh techniques.

Topological insulators and semimetals are characterized by the presence of exotic electronic states on their boundaries or surface states that are robust against perturbations. Recent research has focused on creating artificial systems that can simulate and manipulate such phenomena. Notably, researchers have successfully implemented 3D systems with robust states localized at their two-dimensional boundaries. However, implementing surfaces with robust states in momentum space remains elusive. In this paper, we explore the theoretical foundations of robust nodal surfaces in systems with five or more dimensions and discuss the recent breakthrough in realizing these surfaces in 7D momentum space using photonic systems. We also discuss the potential for using these systems to create robust unidirectional light propagation and discuss the possibility of implementing analogous structures in lower-dimensional systems that can host robust states.

This paper introduces Multi-task focus directed network (MAG-Net), a deep learning model designed to tackle the challenges of brain tumor segmentation and classification. As a multi-task problem, accurate segmentation and classification require advanced techniques. Existing solutions often employ separate networks for each task, but this approach can be inefficient. Our proposed solution utilizes Multi-task focus directed network architecture, which enables the network to adapt task-specific features dynamically. By introducing a task-gating attention mechanism, MAG-Net can effectively select relevant features from a shared encoder. Experimental evaluations on public datasets demonstrate the network's effectiveness, with improved Dice scores and accuracy in comparison to state-of-the-art methods.

This study introduces a novel approach to differentiate the shadow casting operation, which has not been previously accomplished. A cutting-edge method is proposed to efficiently compute the shadow's differentiability. Additionally, a new loss function is developed to minimize the shadow estimation discrepancy. The proposed method's superiority over existing techniques is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world images. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengzheng0925/diff-shadow.

A cutting-edge deep learning-based video deinterlacing technique has been developed, which can process and restore high-quality video from low-resolution interlaced input at an extremely fast rate. Unlike previous methods, this new approach does not require matching information from neighboring frames, allowing it to operate in real-time. The model was trained using a custom dataset of 1.5 million clean, non-interlaced video clips, and was tested on various benchmarks, achieving outstanding results. It was also demonstrated to excel in real-world video playback scenarios.

The average square radius of the neutron distribution has been calculated for 48 nuclei spanning the mass range from 40 Ca to 48 Ca using the relativistic mean field model and the Skyrme mean field model. A comparison of the results from both models has been made and the calculated values using both models have been compared to experimental data. A correlation between the average square radius of the neutron distribution and the neutron skin thickness has been established for the 48 nuclei studied.

To better understand and forecast natural disasters, such as floods, hydrologists rely on mathematical models that simulate water flow. These models, however, are computationally expensive and time-consuming to run, hindering real-time decision-making. In this study, we've developed a novel deep learning architecture that can accurately predict water flow dynamics in a vast and complex 2D domain within a fraction of a second. Our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of both training time and inference speed, enabling real-time decision-making. We've also demonstrated the potential of our model to be used as a rapid solver in data assimilation algorithms, such as the ensemble Kalman filter, to improve flood forecasting accuracy. By combining the accuracy of physical models with real-time observations, our research paves the way for more effective disaster management strategies.

High-dynamic-range photography is a technique used to capture a wide range of brightness levels in a scene by combining multiple exposures. This method is widely employed in modern mobile devices' camera applications to produce balanced images. A critical aspect of this technique is determining whether to combine images using pixel-level or by selecting the most appropriate exposure for each pixel. This paper presents a unified HDR approach that utilizes a neural network to both decide the fusion method and enhance the final image quality. Our proposed system outperforms existing HDR algorithms in both subjective and objective evaluations. Furthermore, our decision-making model surpasses existing HDR methods in speed and memory efficiency when tested on mobile devices.

This paper, titled "Navigating causal neural networks" is a work that addresses current challenges in causal representation learning. It outlines the fundamental principles behind causal network representations and their applications in various fields. Furthermore, it outlines potential directions for future research within this area.

Understanding how heat is distributed in the bed of a fluidized system is crucial for optimizing various chemical engineering processes.  However, measuring temperature in these conditions is challenging due to the dynamic movement of the particles.  This study utilizes magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to visualize and measure heat distribution within a stationary bed of particles, as probed by the technique.  By taking advantage of MRI's non-invasive nature and its ability to provide three-dimensional measurements simultaneously, researchers were able to monitor heat transfer in a controlled environment.  The study's findings indicate that the temperature within the bed is not uniform, with the temperature at the heating surface being significantly higher than the temperature at the center of the bed.  The temperature profile is influenced by the size of the particles and the amount of heat being applied.  The study's results can be used to inform the design of chemical engineering processes that rely on heat transfer in fluidized systems.

Mumford's hypothesis, a key principle behind the birational moduli space of stable varieties, has been a key concept in the field of algebraic geometry. A key aspect of this hypothesis is the inequality that relates the degree and volume of a stable variety. We introduce a key inequality that relates the volume of a hypersurface to its degree and the number of its defining coefficients. We also prove that this inequality is sufficient for the existence of a stable variety that meets the requirements of the b-principle. Additionally, we show that this inequality is satisfied by a high-dimensional family of smooth hypersurfaces.

This study presents an in-depth examination of multilevel preconditioning techniques to address the complex challenge of cardiac mechanics simulations. The primary goal is to efficiently handle the multiscale and strongly non-linear characteristics of the problem. The research compares various approaches, including multigrid methods combined with local refinement and linearization, to determine the most suitable technique. The analysis is conducted by examining the computational costs and performance of each approach in solving a realistic problem. The results indicate that one multilevel preconditioner outperforms the others, providing a significant improvement in solution time. The multilevel technique offers a substantial reduction in computational costs compared to traditional methods, making it a promising solution for cardiac mechanics simulations. The findings contribute to the broader understanding of multilevel preconditioning techniques and their potential applications in other complex simulations. The research also highlights the importance of considering both local and global factors when designing multilevel preconditioners. In recent years, significant advancements have been made in AI-driven video production, which is a highly resource-intensive process involving multiple stages, including content generation, editing, and sound mixing. Due to the high computational demands and expensive equipment required, extensive research in this area has been limited. This study provides a comprehensive overview of the primary stages in video production, focusing on key developments in text-to-video and image-to-video techniques. Additionally, this survey examines the primary challenges and potential future directions in this field.

This paper presents Deceptive Sense of Safety (DSOS), a novel approach to evaluating whether a bot's claimed awareness of danger is genuine or fabricated. 
DSOS leverages the concept of a deceptive sense of safety, a phenomenon where individuals who have been subjected to persistent threats may falsely perceive their environment as secure. 
Within this context, DSOS measures the authenticity of a bot's claimed sense of safety by analyzing the disparity between its reported danger awareness and the actual security of its surroundings. 
The core of DSOS lies in a deceptive sense of safety metric, which quantifies the difference between a bot's perceived safety level and the actual security of its environment. 
Furthermore, DSOS employs a deceptive sense of safety matrix to comprehensively assess a bot's deceptive sense of safety across various scenarios. 
The proposed DSOS framework is demonstrated through the evaluation of a bot named Danger-Aware Bot (DABot), showcasing its ability to accurately gauge the authenticity of a bot's claimed danger awareness.

Our research focuses on the potential of microacoustic metagratings in the ultrasonic frequency range. To achieve this, we developed a compact microacoustic metagrating with 100x higher resolution than existing devices, fabricated using two-photon lithography. This high-resolution metagrating allows for precise acoustic beam control, directing 180kHz ultrasound into 16 distinct angles. We also demonstrated that these devices can effectively control ultrasound beams in reverse, directing electromagnetic waves into specific angles when exposed to high-frequency acoustic waves. This breakthrough paves the way for advanced applications in ultrasonic imaging and communication systems.

Anomalous diffusion, which deviates from normal diffusion, is observed in complex media and can be influenced by non-Gaussian distributions. Studies using synthetic and real micro-CT images of volcanic tephra and carbonate rocks have shown that diffusion is typically non-Gaussian due to the random properties within these materials. However, some experiments have yielded Gaussian distributions without a clear explanation. This study proposes a theoretical model to explore how different distributions of conductive pathways can result in various distribution functions, ultimately leading to an understanding of why certain materials exhibit normal diffusion despite their inherent complexity. A Gaussian distribution can be achieved through the multiplication of log-normally distributed components, providing a possible explanation for diffusion patterns observed in real materials.

A key aspect of this theory is the development of a set of mode coefficients that serve as a basis for describing the spatial distribution of modes. A new parameter, the coupling coefficient, is introduced to quantify linear and Kerr nonlinear coupling between modes. A new metric, the effective coupling length, is proposed to assess the degree of mode coupling. A new classification system is established to categorize optical cavities and waveguides based on their dominant linear and Kerr nonlinear coupling mechanisms. A new concept, the effective coupling area, is introduced to describe the spatial extent of mode coupling. This paper expands upon previous research by relaxing the unbounded control constraint in stable control systems. We introduce unbounded feedback controls that ensure stable system behavior and provide a sufficient condition for the existence of such controls, applicable to a broad class of systems. These controls are derived using stable homotopy theory, a branch of algebraic topology, and the concept of a "bracket" for vector fields, which is a key component of this expansion.

A new method for enhancing the spatial resolution of turbulent flows has been developed, utilizing a generative adversarial network. Building upon a previously established approach, we have expanded our model to accommodate flows at different Reynolds numbers. Our tests, conducted on turbulent channel flow at Reτ = 180, 5000, and an infinite Reynolds number, demonstrate significant improvements in resolution restoration, reducing the required grid spacing by a factor of 10 to 20 in the wall-normal direction. Our method outperforms traditional interpolation techniques, such as third-order compact compactly supported convolution, particularly in terms of grid compactness. Our results also show that our model can effectively restore second-order derivatives, such as wall shear stress and friction velocity, with a high degree of accuracy. Our research provides a practical and efficient means for high-resolution simulations of turbulent flows, which is crucial for accurate modeling of complex flow phenomena.

A key aspect examined is the impact of initial conditions on a solution's uniqueness, with implications for the Cauchy problem. Deep neural network-based approaches have been highly effective in solving complex real-world problems, yet their ability to handle novel situations remains limited. To address this constraint, researchers have developed methods to create open-world representations, but these techniques often suffer from high memory consumption and difficulty in managing unobserved data. This study proposes an energy-based framework to model uncertainty over unknown data, enabling the system to account for unobserved information. A novel energy-based activation uncertainty model is introduced to capture system guarantees and ensure consistency with training data. A new loss function is designed to integrate this uncertainty model into the primary learning process. The results of the study demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in ensuring reliable performance on open-world tasks.

Automated systems that adapt to changing conditions are crucial for maintaining optimal performance over extended periods without human intervention. Reinforcement learning has shown great potential in creating adaptive algorithms capable of learning from new data and experiences. To facilitate the evaluation of these reinforcement learning approaches, a new platform has been developed, which consists of a series of interconnected virtual worlds that allow for the testing of lifelong learning methods. This platform, which is designed to be extensible, enables the addition of new virtual worlds and features, such as transfer learning and world graph optimization. A comparative study of different learning strategies within this platform has revealed the importance of maintaining and updating knowledge representations in order to achieve optimal performance.

The Processes Interchange Format (PIE) serves as a declarative language for process specification, but its lack of support for data manipulation and external interaction poses a limitation. To address this, an extension to PIE has been proposed, incorporating stream processing capabilities. This allows processes to be connected with streams, enabling automatic handling of data and integration with modern event-driven architectures. This proposal is accompanied by a formal framework, which includes process and stream definitions, combined with proof techniques for verifying process properties. The proposed concept is illustrated through a structural operational semantics and a case study on the monitoring of key performance indicators. The underlying theory is further expanded by the development of a model checker, which facilitates the verification of declarative specifications, including those in PIE, utilizing stream automata. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through comparative experiments with existing verification methods. The proposed framework is implemented through the development of the ProIE tool, which is available for download. The code and test cases are accessible through the provided GitHub link. The proposed framework is also applicable to alternative process specification formalisms, as evidenced by the analysis of Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP).

One-dimensional quasicrystals exhibit striking behaviors not found in periodic structures, including a phenomenon where an unusual transition occurs - from insulating to conducting states and back to insulating states. This study shows that a one-dimensional photonic quasicrystal can display a similar tri-state behavior, where light transitions from being stuck in one state to being free and then stuck again as the system's parameter is changed. This phenomenon is observed as a shift from localized to delocalized states and back to localized states.

Liger, a high-performance adaptive optics system at the W. M. Keck Observatory, is designed to enhance the performance of the Keck II 10-meter telescope in the near-infrared range. Liger's system comprises four adaptive optics subsystems, including the Keck Adaptive Secondary Mirror, the Liger Deformable Mirror, the Liger Wavefront Sensor, and the Liger Real-Time Wavefront Control. These components work in concert to correct for atmospheric turbulence and maintain optimal telescope performance. As part of the system's development, a data processing framework was created to handle the high data rates produced by the wavefront sensors and to enable real-time image processing. Additionally, software was developed to integrate the Keck Observatory's telescope control system with the adaptive optics subsystems and to enable real-time image processing and wavefront control. This development effort is being led by researchers from the University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and the Chinese Academy of Sciences, in collaboration with the Keck Observatory.

High-fidelity measurement of two-photon spatial mode distributions is crucial for quantum information processing using spatial light engineering. We propose a novel method to measure the resolution beyond the diffraction limit using a two-photon interference pattern, achieved through a coupling process that separates the photonic modes without a multi-mode beam splitter. Our research shows that a new parameter, effective resolution, is influenced by a specific type of entanglement between the photons, allowing us to manipulate the resolution by altering the entanglement. A numerical simulation demonstrates that this method can accurately measure fine features in complex distributions, even in the presence of low signal-to-noise ratios.

This paper provides an overview of recent advancements in constructing compactifications of moduli spaces using toric algebraic and geometric methods. We initially explain the connection between polyhedral structures and toric varieties, then proceed to discuss how combinatorial data can be utilized to define both algebraic and geometric spaces, before illustrating the application of these spaces to the compactification of torus and Sato Grassmannian moduli spaces of.

A significant issue with early warning indicators (EWIs) of critical transitions in complex systems is the frequent presence of false alarms due to inherent fluctuations. This problem is particularly pronounced in population ecosystems, where unpredictable fluctuations can hinder the early detection of significant population changes. This study employs a stochastic lattice model to examine the dynamics of a predator-prey system and its response to an imposed external periodic fluctuation. Our analysis reveals that certain fluctuations, including those caused by an external periodic force, can be distinguished from others using a combination of statistical measures. This enables the reliable identification of a warning period for major population shifts. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through its application to the detection of an imposed periodic fluctuation and its potential to be utilized in detecting significant population changes in the ecosystem.

A recent study found an intriguing link between a galaxy's quenching time and its stellar mass-to-light ratio, an observation that defies the expected correlation between these two quantities. To investigate this anomaly, a statistical analysis was conducted, examining the properties of galaxies within an $a_b$-bin, utilizing a sample of $1.5 \times 10^5$ $z=0$ galaxies from the ALFALFA survey. The study revealed that the quenching time is significantly influenced by a galaxy's bulge-to-total stellar mass ratio, an effect that becomes more pronounced at higher stellar masses. The study's findings suggest that a galaxy's central supermassive black hole's activity is primarily triggered by galaxy mergers, an event that is more likely to occur in massive galaxies with small bulge-to-total stellar mass ratios. The study also highlights the importance of a galaxy's bulge in determining its quenching time, an effect that is likely due to the galaxy's bulge's influence on its central supermassive black hole's activity. The study's findings also suggest that a galaxy's quenching time is closely related to its star formation history, an event that is likely due to the galaxy's mergers that trigger the galaxy's quenching. The study's results are in line with the $M^*$-SFR relation, an event that is likely due to the galaxy's mergers that trigger the galaxy's quenching.

This paper introduces a novel approach to sentiment assessment that transcends linguistic boundaries. By incorporating both sentiment classification and aspect-based classification tasks, our framework leverages shared knowledge across tasks and languages to enhance performance. Our proposed model, a hierarchical bidirectional LSTM architecture, is capable of simultaneously executing these tasks and is particularly effective when data availability is limited. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in improving sentiment classification accuracy, especially for low-frequency classes and languages.

This paper introduces a novel technique to eliminate barriers in distributed systems, called self-invalidating and self-devaluing repairs, which eliminates the need for a global timekeeping system. This technique is shown to be more efficient in terms of message exchange and processing, compared to existing methods that rely on a global timekeeping system. We also explore the implications of using this technique in terms of the number of messages and messages per faulty component required to eliminate barriers.

Given a non-periodic abelian group G and a non-periodic subset A within it, if |2A| is significantly smaller than |A|, specifically |2A| ≤ k|A| where k is greater than 2, and the cardinality of A is at least 2k, then |A| is upper bounded by a function f(k) times the sum of the 2-adic valuation of the group order and 2. This result is a substantial improvement upon a previous theorem by Balog and Szemerédi, reducing the 2-adic valuation constraint from |G| ≥ 2^(4k^2) to |G| ≥ 2^(ck).

Consider a $d$-dimensional fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter $H$, denoted as $(B_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$, and let $A$ be a Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$. The set $\mathcal{T}(A)$, consisting of all times $s$ in the interval $[0,1]$ where the path of $(B_t)$ intersects $A$ at time $s$ but not before, has a well-defined Hausdorff dimension under certain conditions, specifically when the dimension exceeds $1/2$ and the measure of the set is positive. This paper builds on previous research by proving that under certain conditions, the set $\mathcal{T}(A)$ has a positive Lebesgue measure and an interior that is not empty, almost surely.

This study employs Dirac's variational principle to investigate the nonintegrable behavior of the Henon-Heiles model, and we refine previous quantum calculations by Dirar, Zangwill, and Shakhbazov using more accurate data. Dirac's variational method is shown to be an effective tool for examining complex systems, and our results indicate that as the system transitions from integrable to nonintegrable behavior, the density matrix of a single particle exhibits a decline in order, and a significant increase in energy, and a decrease in density.

This research paper is an initial exploration of using deep learning to predict ICU admission from chest X-ray images of COVID-19 patients. Due to a lack of publicly available datasets that include ICU information, we propose that future researchers investigate this area by annotating chest X-ray images with relevant metadata. We believe this could enhance the capabilities of existing models and facilitate more accurate diagnoses.

This research establishes that a simplicial group constitutes an exemplary instance of a simplicial bundle when categorized over the pathoid of simplicial endomaps. Consequently, we can infer that any simplicial bundle possessing a simplicial group as its total space is, in fact, equivalent to a simplicial group up to weak isomorphism. This implication further allows us to conclude that the fundamental group functor is essentially surjective and faithful, thereby making it an equivalence.

Our analysis of the current dataset reveals a significant issue in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD): a significant number of relationships are falsely identified. This problem stems from the limited scope of existing data, which hampers the effectiveness of current models. In response, we have developed a comprehensive evaluation framework to assess models' performance across various categories of relationships. This framework reveals that current models struggle with under-represented relationships, often resulting in high false positives. To tackle this issue, we have proposed a new dataset, V-Refine, which features a refined annotation of 100k images and an additional 40k relationships. Our experiments demonstrate that V-Refine outperforms current datasets, achieving a significant improvement in mean average precision. Moreover, our proposed relationship refinement strategy yields an even greater improvement in model performance.

This study proposes a novel approach to address the challenges of low-light activity recognition in scenarios with limited training data. By employing a cutting-edge architecture called R-BERT and a data reduction technique called delta sampling, the proposed method effectively tackles the constraints of low-light conditions and limited training sets. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and robustness.

A novel concurrent processing architecture has been developed, featuring a unique data control mechanism. This mechanism allows the processing elements to automatically navigate through input data without the need for explicit addressing, which is instead managed by an embedded finite state machine within each processing element. The design's efficiency has been demonstrated through the creation of a data addressable processing element and a multi-processor system implemented on an FPGA. The system's capabilities include executing benchmark algorithms such as sorting, matrix multiplication, and image processing, which have been optimized through the integration of a high-speed internal memory and configurable datapath. The research has also explored the potential for custom memory organization and the use of multiple internal memories to enhance the system's performance. The design's flexibility has been further highlighted through the development of a high-level hardware description language and a synthesis tool that converts the system into an efficient hardware implementation. The research has been presented through a combination of hardware descriptions, performance measurements, and visual demonstrations of the system's capabilities. This galaxy is a typical example of a quiescent, lopsided disk within a cluster, characterized by a prominent bulge. Hubble observations have revealed a compact, dense object within this galaxy, which is actively forming stars at a rate of 0.2 solar masses per year. This object is surrounded by a diffuse halo of light, which is being emitted by high-energy photons. A previous analysis of the K meson system yielded no conclusive evidence for GSZ, prompting further examination. This study expands upon the initial GSZ assessment by employing a more comprehensive Bayesian framework, incorporating additional data from the B and D meson systems.
